What AI does well right now, and what it doesn't, is covered in the article on [AI for social media](@vestacka-inteligencija-za-drustvene-mreze).

## Frequently asked questions

### Is the price per post or per month?

Usually per month, for an agreed number of posts and networks. A price per post makes sense for one-off jobs, such as a campaign before an opening, but for ongoing management a monthly agreement is clearer.

### Is the ad budget included in the management fee?

Almost never. Ad money goes directly to Meta, Google or TikTok from your card, and management is a separate service. If an offer says otherwise, ask how much of the amount actually goes on ads.

### How much does it cost just to create posts, without publishing them?

Less, because comments, messages and reports drop out. But be careful: posts with nobody answering the comments lose their point, because customers' questions go unanswered.

### Is it worth paying annually?

It's worth it when you're sure you'll stick with the same way of working. With tools, an annual subscription is usually much cheaper per month. With agencies, ask for a trial period of two to three months before you sign an annual contract.

posts.title: Social media for restaurants and cafés: what to post to bring guests in
posts.seoTitle: Social media for restaurants and cafés: a guide
posts.description: How a restaurant or café should run Instagram, Facebook and Google Business Profile: food photos on your phone, a weekly plan, menus, bookings and reviews.
posts.excerpt: For hospitality, social media is your shop window. Which networks to choose, how to photograph food on your phone, a sample week of posts, and the mistakes that send guests next door.
posts.body:
For a restaurant or café, most guests come from **Instagram with good photos of the food and the space, Google Business Profile with accurate opening hours and reviews, and Facebook for events and the local crowd**. Post three times a week and put the daily specials in Stories. What matters most is that the picture makes people hungry and that a guest knows straight away how to book or get there.

:::ukratko
- Instagram, Google Business Profile and Facebook are the basics for hospitality.
- **A real photo of your own food**, in daylight, is worth more than any stock image.
- Daily specials go in Stories, and dishes, the space and the people go in posts.
- Booking must take one tap: a message, a call or a link.
- Accurate opening hours and replies to reviews are a must, not an option.
:::

## Which networks, and why?

**Instagram is your shop window.** People look at the food, the space and the atmosphere before they decide where to go. A profile with lovely photos of dishes and full tables sells better than any ad.

Google Business Profile is where the decision gets made. “Restaurant near me”, “café with garden Dorćol” (a Belgrade neighbourhood), “breakfast Novi Sad”: the people typing these are looking for a place right now. Opening hours, photos, the menu and reviews on your profile decide it. How to run it is covered in the article on [Google Business Profile posts](@google-poslovni-profil-objave).

Facebook is good for events, local groups and an older audience. If you put on live music, tastings or parties, a Facebook event still works.

TikTok and Reels are for places that have something to show in motion: cooking, cocktail making, latte art. They're not a must, but they can bring in lots of new people from around town.

## Photographing food on your phone

You don't need a photographer for every post. You need a few habits:

- Daylight, a table by the window, no flash.
- Two angles almost always work: from above for plates and bowls, from the side for burgers, cakes and drinks.
- A clean plate and a clean table. A crumb on the rim shows up more in a photo than it does at the table.
- Take the photo straight away, before the dish loses its shine.
- People in the frame, such as a hand holding a cup or cutting into something, bring the picture to life, but only with permission.

**Stock photos of food are a bad idea.** A guest comes in, gets a different-looking plate and feels cheated. Always show your own.

!slika:drustvene-mreze-za-restorane-i-kafice-1

## What to post: a sample week

!slika:drustvene-mreze-za-restorane-i-kafice-info

A bistro in Kragujevac, with three posts a week plus Stories every day.

| Day | Where | What |
|---|---|---|
| Monday | Instagram Stories | dish of the day and its price |
| Tuesday | Instagram and Facebook | short video: how the dish of the week is made |
| Thursday | Instagram, Facebook, Google | weekend menu and bookings |
| Saturday | Instagram | photo of a full room or the team |
| Every day | Instagram Stories | daily specials, free tables, guests (with permission) |

Thursday is the day for the weekend, because that's when people plan where they'll go on Friday and Saturday, and book a table while there's still room. Monday and Tuesday are quieter, so they're good for a story about a dish and the kitchen. There are more ideas in the [list of 40 post ideas](@ideje-za-objave-na-drustvenim-mrezama), and you can turn this week into a whole month by following the article on [the content calendar](@plan-objava-za-drustvene-mreze).

## Your menu on social media

Your menu should be easy to find. People ask “what do you have?” and “how much is it?” more often than anything else. Good solutions:

- Instagram Highlights on your profile with the menu by category,
- the menu on your Google Business Profile, with prices,
- a photo of the daily specials in Stories every morning.

Avoid a menu that's a blurry photo of a sheet of paper, or a PDF that won't open on a phone. If your prices change, change them everywhere on the same day. **An old price on social media is the most common cause of a bad impression** at the very start of a visit.

## Bookings and messages

Every post should have **a clear next step**: “Book by message”, “Call 064 ...”, “Booking link in our bio”. If a guest has to hunt for your number, they'll go to someone who gave them theirs.

Reply to messages quickly: within a couple of minutes during opening hours, and by the next morning outside them. An automatic reply with your opening hours and a booking link helps when you're busy. Reply to comments under your posts within the first hour, because that's when a post gets the most attention.

## Reviews

For restaurants and cafés, Google reviews count almost as much as photos. Ask happy guests for one, on the bill, with a QR code on the table or through a word from the waiter. Reply to every review: thanks for praise, calm and specific answers to criticism. Guests read the replies as much as the reviews, because they show how you behave when something goes wrong. Don't delete or report bad reviews just because they're bad. People notice, and it looks worse than the criticism itself.

## The most common social media mistakes in hospitality

- Wrong opening hours on Google, especially over the holidays.
- Nothing but promotions and discounts, with no dishes and no people.
- Dark photos taken in the evening under yellow light.
- A menu that can't be found or is out of date.
- A profile that goes quiet for a month and then posts five things in one day.
- Posts with no call to book and no address.

A rhythm of three posts a week is easier to keep up than it looks, especially if you write all the captions in one go. The numbers for each network are in the article on [how often to post](@koliko-cesto-objavljivati-na-drustvenim-mrezama).

## How does Sova help restaurants and cafés?

Sova reads your restaurant's or café's website and remembers your menu, prices, opening hours, address and tone. From that it makes a plan for the month and writes posts for Instagram, Facebook and Google Business Profile: for Instagram with a call to action and hashtags, for Facebook in a chattier style, for Google practically, with your opening hours. It takes photos of dishes from your Gallery, because the food people see has to be your own. You review the draft and approve it, and Sova publishes it at the right time.

If you have several venues or work for several restaurants and cafés, all the brands sit in one account, each with its own tone and calendar. You can see how that looks on the [home page](/#features). You can start a trial [for free, with no card](/register).

## Frequently asked questions

### Which social networks are best for a restaurant?

Instagram and Google Business Profile are the basics, and Facebook helps with events and the local crowd. TikTok is an extra for places that have time for short videos.

### How often should a restaurant post?

Three posts a week and Stories almost every day. Post the weekend menu on Thursday, when people are planning their night out.

### How do I photograph food on my phone?

In daylight by a window, from above for plates and from the side for burgers and cakes, without flash and straight after the food is served. Clean the table and the rim of the plate before you take the photo.

### Should I post prices?

Yes. Guests look for prices before they come, and a clear price saves time for them and for your staff. Just make sure the prices on social media are the same as on the menu.

posts.title: Brand voice on social media: how to sound like you, every time
posts.seoTitle: Brand voice on social media: a guide and template
posts.description: What brand voice is, how to describe it on a single page and apply it on every network. A template with six questions and the same post in two voices.
posts.excerpt: Brand voice is the way you sound in every post. How to write it down on one page, what goes into the template and how to stay the same on every network.
posts.body:
Brand voice is **the way your business sounds in every post, message and reply**: whether you address customers formally or informally, whether you're serious or playful, which words you use and which ones you never use. When it's written down on one page, everyone who writes for you, person or AI, sounds the same. When it isn't, every post sounds as if someone else wrote it.

:::ukratko
- Brand voice is your personality in text, and tone is how that personality adapts to the situation.
- Write it down on **a single page**: six questions are enough.
- In Serbian, first decide between the formal and informal “you” (vi or ti), and between the Latin and Cyrillic alphabets.
- The same personality on every network, with a different tone on LinkedIn and TikTok.
- You test a voice with examples, not adjectives.
:::

## Voice and tone are not the same thing

Your voice is your personality, and it doesn't change. Tone is how that personality sounds in different situations. A bakery can have a warm, playful voice. When it announces that it's closed because of a breakdown, the tone is more serious, but it's still the same bakery and it still sounds warm.

This matters because of the networks. On LinkedIn you'll be more serious than on TikTok. That's a change of tone. If on LinkedIn you sound like a different company, that's a change of voice, and customers notice it.

## Why does brand voice matter at all?

People buy from the businesses they recognise. When someone reads your post and thinks “this sounds like them” before they've even seen the profile name, you've done it. That only happens when every post sounds the same.

The second reason is practical. If your posts are written by you, your staff, an agency and an AI tool, without written rules you end up with four different brands. **One page of rules** fixes that in an hour.

## Six questions for a brand voice document

!slika:glas-brenda-na-drustvenim-mrezama-info

1. Who are we talking to? One sentence about the customer: who they are, how old they are, what matters to them.
2. Vi or ti? In Serbian this is **the first decision**, because the language has a formal “you” (vi) and an informal one (ti). Vi is more polite and the safer choice for services and companies. Ti feels closer and works for a younger audience, cafés and gyms.
3. Which three words describe us? For example “warm, expert, brief” or “cheerful, direct, local”.
4. Which words do we use? Product names, local expressions, technical terms customers understand.
5. Which words do we never use? Empty advertising phrases, jargon, words your customers don't like.
6. An example of a good post and a bad one. This is the most important item, because adjectives mean different things to different people, and an example doesn't.

Add a few practical rules as well: emojis or not, exclamation marks or not, Latin or Cyrillic script, and how the brand name is written.

## The same text in two voices

Look at how the same information sounds in two different voices. Both versions are correct. The question is which one is yours.

| Voice | Post about new opening hours |
|---|---|
| Polite, expert | “From 1 December we're also open on Saturdays, from 9:00 to 14:00. You can book an appointment by phone or by message.” |
| Warm, playful | “A Saturday without your hair done? Not with us. From 1 December we're open on Saturdays too, 9 to 2. Send us a message or give us a call, and we'll keep a spot for you.” |

Notice that both versions contain the same facts: the date, the day, the hours and how to book. **Voice changes how you sound, not what you say.**

!slika:glas-brenda-na-drustvenim-mrezama-1

## Brand voice in Serbian: decisions of its own

Serbian asks for a few decisions that English doesn't. They matter whenever you post in Serbian, for customers in Serbia or the wider region:

- Vi or ti, and whether to write Vi with a capital letter. Serbian has a formal “you” and an informal one, much like French vous and tu. In posts for a wide audience a lower-case “vi” is the norm, and a capital “Vi” is kept for addressing one person directly.
- Latin or Cyrillic. Serbian is written in both alphabets. You can use both, but consistently, by network or by type of post.
- Ekavian or Ijekavian, if you have customers from across the region. These are two standard variants of the language that spell some words differently, such as mleko and mlijeko for “milk”.
- Gender: how you address people when you don't know whether a man or a woman is reading. Serbian adjectives and past-tense verbs change with gender, and sentences like “zakažite termin” (“book an appointment”) avoid the problem.

You make these decisions once and write them into your rules. After that you don't have to think about them again. If you write in English, the closest equivalents are how formal you sound and whether you use British or American spelling.

## How do you stay the same on every network?

The personality stays, while the length, tone and format change:

- Instagram: shorter, more visual, with a clear call to action.
- Facebook: more conversational, a little longer, with an invitation to send a message.
- LinkedIn: a more serious tone, the story behind the business, your expertise. There's more on this in the article on [LinkedIn company pages](@linkedin-stranica-firme).
- TikTok: the most relaxed, spoken as if in conversation. Ideas are in the article on [TikTok for business](@tiktok-za-firme).

The check is simple: when you read posts from three networks one after another, **do they sound like the same person?**

## Brand voice and AI

AI tools write quickly, but without rules they sound like everyone else. That's why a written brand voice is the most important thing you can give an AI. The more specific it is, with examples, the closer the text gets to your own.

In Sova, brand voice has a place of its own. You can write it yourself or press “Suggest from sources”, and Sova drafts a suggestion from what it has read on your website, in a brand PDF and in your earlier posts. Once you approve it, the brand voice goes into every piece of writing, so every post, carousel and reply follows the same rules. Sova writes in Serbian, in Latin or Cyrillic script, and in English, and it sticks to one language within a post. You can see how this looks in practice in the [features section](/#features).

What AI does well, and where it needs your hand, is covered in the article on [AI for social media](@vestacka-inteligencija-za-drustvene-mreze). How to apply your brand voice to a caption, step by step, is explained in the article on [how to write an Instagram caption](@kako-napisati-opis-za-instagram-objavu).

## How do you know the voice is working?

After a month, run two tests. First, read your last ten posts in a row. Do they sound like one brand? Second, ask two loyal customers to describe your profile in three words. If they use words similar to the ones you wrote down, the voice is working. If they don't, compare the two and add examples to your rules.

Brand voice is part of a bigger picture of what you post and how. For the start of that picture, see the [guide to social media management for small business](@vodjenje-drustvenih-mreza-za-mali-biznis).

## Frequently asked questions

### What is brand voice?

The way your business sounds in posts, messages and replies: how you address people, your vocabulary, how serious you are, your humour. It stays the same on every network, while the tone adapts to the situation.

### Should I address customers formally (vi) or informally (ti)?

It depends on your audience. Vi, the formal form, is the safer choice for services, healthcare, companies and older audiences. Ti, the informal one, works for younger audiences, cafés and gyms. What matters is that the choice is the same in every post.

### How long should a brand voice document be?

One page is enough: six answers and two or three examples. Nobody reads a longer document, and a shorter one doesn't cover the basic decisions.

### Can AI write in my voice?

Yes, if you give it clear rules and examples. Without them it writes in a generic voice that sounds like an ad for anyone at all.

posts.title: Google Business Profile posts: the forgotten network that brings in calls
posts.seoTitle: Google Business Profile posts: a guide for businesses
posts.description: How to post on your Google Business Profile: updates, offers and events, up to 1,500 characters, photos, a call button and how often to post.
posts.excerpt: Everyone who searches for you on Maps and in Google Search sees your Google Business Profile. The three types of post, how often to post, what to write and why consistency matters even more here than on Instagram.
posts.body:
Google Business Profile posts are **short updates, offers and events that people see when they search for you on Google Search and Maps**. A post can be up to 1,500 characters long, with a photo and a button such as “Call now” or “Book”. For a local business, one post a week is enough to make the profile look alive, and the people who find you there are usually ready to buy straight away.

:::ukratko
- The people who find you on your Google profile are already looking for a service nearby.
- **One post a week** keeps the profile alive, because an ordinary update doesn't stay at the top for long.
- Three types of post: update, offer and event.
- The first sentences and the action button do most of the work.
- Up-to-date opening hours and replies to reviews are worth as much as the posts.
:::

## Why does your Google profile matter, and why is it so often forgotten?

When someone types “bakery Liman” (a neighbourhood in Novi Sad) or “hairdresser near me” into their phone, Google shows a map and a few profiles. These people aren't scrolling out of boredom. They're looking for somewhere to go right now. That's why a profile with up-to-date opening hours, good photos, reviews and fresh posts is often where the decision gets made.

Even so, many businesses set up a profile once and forget about it. The last post is two years old, the opening hours are out of date, the reviews have no replies. That's why this is a network where **a little effort gives you a big advantage** over the competition.

## Three types of post

!slika:google-poslovni-profil-objave-info

An update is a general post: a new service, new opening hours, a product photo, a tip. It's the most common type and the one you should post regularly.

An offer has a title, a validity period and, if you like, a code or terms. It's good for time-limited promotions, for example “10% off haircuts on Tuesdays in December”. It stays visible until the end of the period.

An event has a title and a start and end date and time. A workshop, a tasting, an opening, an open day. It's visible until the day of the event.

An ordinary update is most prominent for a short time after you post it, so **consistency matters more than volume**. One update every week means there's always something fresh on your profile.

## What should you write in a post?

The rules are similar to Instagram, with one difference: people on Google are looking for information, not entertainment. Write practically.

1. The first sentence says the main thing: what's new and why it matters to the customer.
2. The second and third sentences give the details: price, deadline, how to order.
3. The button leads to an action that makes sense: a call, a booking, an order or your website.
4. The photo is real, taken in your own space, and well lit.

Only the start of the text shows in the preview, so the key information goes at the beginning. Hashtags serve no purpose here, so leave them out. An example: “From Monday we're also baking spelt bread, every morning from 7:00. Price: 260 RSD. Call us and we'll put one aside for you.” Short, useful, with a reason to call.

## Photos on your profile

Photos on your profile don't live only in posts. Google also shows the photos of your premises, products and team that you add to the profile, as well as the ones your customers add. Add new photos at least once a month: the shop window, the interior, your products, the people who work there (with their consent). The photo people see on the map often decides whether they click on you or on the place next door.

!slika:google-poslovni-profil-objave-1

## Reviews and replies

Reviews aren't posts, but they do the same job: they show that the profile is alive and that someone cares. Reply to every one, briefly and personally. When someone praises you, thank them and mention something specific from their review. When someone criticises you, reply calmly, admit what's true and offer a solution, without arguing in public.

Ask happy customers for a review. The easiest moment is right after the service, with a sentence and a link, or with a QR code on the receipt. Don't offer a reward for a review and don't buy reviews, because that breaks Google's rules and can put your profile at risk.

## Opening hours and holidays

The most common mistake on a Google profile isn't a bad post. It's the wrong opening hours. A customer turns up, the door is locked, and Google said “open”. A customer like that rarely gives you a second chance.

Before every holiday, enter special opening hours: New Year, Orthodox Christmas (7 January), Easter, Labour Day (1 May), and your slava (the feast of the patron saint a family or business celebrates) if you close that day. **Post an update as well** with the same information, so people see it in your posts too.

## How often should you post?

For most local businesses, **one post a week** is the right amount, plus offers and events when you have them. That's four to five posts a month, about fifteen minutes a week. If you fit this into the same plan as Instagram and Facebook and [schedule it in advance](@zakazivanje-objava-na-instagramu-i-facebooku), there's even less work, because it's the same news rewritten in a more practical way. How to put all your networks into one schedule is covered in the article on [the content calendar](@plan-objava-za-drustvene-mreze), and how many posts go on which network in the article on [how often to post](@koliko-cesto-objavljivati-na-drustvenim-mrezama).

## Do posts help you rank higher on Maps?

Google doesn't publish the exact recipe for ranking on Maps. What is known is that three things matter: distance from the person searching, how well the profile matches the search, and how well known and well rated the business is. Posts on their own are no magic wand, but an active, complete profile, with photos, reviews and replies, helps people choose you when they see you. And that's what counts.

## Google Business Profile in Sova

Sova also publishes to Google Business Profile, from the same draft as Instagram and Facebook. The text for Google is written more practically: no hashtags, with opening hours, a price or a deadline when they're in your brand profile, and with a call to action. The image format is adapted for Google. That way one piece of news in the calendar becomes a post on three networks, and your Google profile stops being forgotten.

You can see what the same post looks like for Google and the other networks on the [home page, in the networks section](/#networks). For cafés and restaurants, where the Google profile matters most, we've also written an article on [social media for restaurants and cafés](@drustvene-mreze-za-restorane-i-kafice). If you're just starting out, begin with the [guide for small businesses](@vodjenje-drustvenih-mreza-za-mali-biznis).

## Frequently asked questions

### How many characters can a Google Business Profile post have?

Up to 1,500 characters. Only the beginning shows in the preview, so the most important information goes in the first sentence.

### How long does a post stay visible?

An offer stays visible until the end of the period you set, and an event until the date of the event. An ordinary update is most prominent for a short time after posting, so it's a good idea to post once a week.

### Should I put hashtags on my Google profile?

No. Hashtags on Google Business Profile have no function. Write practically: what's new, the price, the deadline and how people can contact you.

### Do posts affect where I appear on Google Maps?

Google doesn't publish the exact recipe. An active, complete profile with photos, reviews and posts helps people choose you, but the most important factors are distance, how well you match the search and the business's reputation.

posts.title: Instagram hashtags after the limit of five: how to choose them
posts.seoTitle: Instagram hashtags: how many and how to choose them
posts.description: Since December 2025, Instagram allows at most five hashtags per post. How to choose the right five, which ones to avoid and how other networks handle them.
posts.excerpt: With a limit of five hashtags per post, choosing them matters more than ever. A formula with four types of hashtag, what to avoid and the rules for other networks.
posts.body:
Since December 2025, Instagram has allowed **a maximum of five hashtags per post and per Reel**. Accurate hashtags that describe the post and the place work best: for example one local tag (#novisad), one for the topic of the post (#kroasan, Serbian for croissant), one for the type of business (#pekara, bakery) and one of your own (#pekarazrno). These days hashtags help Instagram understand what a post is about. They are no longer the main source of reach.

:::ukratko
- A maximum of five hashtags per post, under the rule Instagram has been introducing since December 2025.
- Accuracy matters more than popularity, because **#love and #instagood don't bring in customers**.
- A good combination: place, topic, type of product or service, your brand.
- Words in the caption help search as much as hashtags do.
- Each network has its own rules: a few on LinkedIn, almost none on Facebook.
:::

## What changed in December 2025?

Instagram announced that it was gradually cutting the number of hashtags you can put in the caption of a post or Reel to five. Before that the limit was 30, and many profiles used every last slot, with a string of generic tags that had nothing to do with the post. The change was reported by many sites, for example [Social Media Today](https://www.socialmediatoday.com/news/instagram-implements-new-limits-on-hashtag-use/808309/).

Adam Mosseri, the head of Instagram, had said before that hashtags don't increase visibility, but that they help sort a post and connect it with similar posts. The limit of five only confirmed what was already true: five accurate tags are worth more than thirty random ones.

## How do you choose the right five?

!slika:hashtagovi-na-instagramu-info

For a local business, this formula works well:

1. One local hashtag: your town or part of town (#novisad, #zemun, #vracar).
2. One or two topical ones: what's in the post (#kroasan, #balayage, #knjigovodstvo).
3. One for the type of business or service (#pekara, #frizerskisalon).
4. One of your own, with your brand name (#pekarazrno), if people use it.

That's five. If you don't have enough good ones, use three. **Fewer accurate tags are better than more wrong ones.**

The examples are in Serbian because the customers of a business in Serbia search in Serbian: #knjigovodstvo means bookkeeping and #frizerskisalon means hair salon. Use the language your own customers search in.

## Which hashtags should you avoid?

- Generic, huge tags (#love, #instagood, #photooftheday). A post gets lost in them within seconds and never reaches the people who would buy.
- Tags that have nothing to do with the post. Instagram may treat them as an attempt to cheat the system and show the post to fewer people.
- The same string of five hashtags on every post. Adapt them to the topic.
- Tags in a foreign language when your customers are local. For a bakery in Serbia, #bakery can bring in followers from all over the world, but not customers to your street.

Before you use a new hashtag, look at what's posted under it. If you see spam or posts that have nothing to do with the topic, skip it.

!slika:hashtagovi-na-instagramu-1

## Do hashtags still affect reach?

A little. These days Instagram decides who sees a post mainly based on **how people react to it** and what they like to watch. Hashtags help the system understand the topic, especially for new profiles it doesn't know much about yet. But if the post is weak, a hashtag won't save it.

So it's smarter to put your time into the first line of the caption and into the picture. How to write a caption people actually read is explained in the article on [how to write an Instagram caption](@kako-napisati-opis-za-instagram-objavu).

## Words in the caption instead of hashtags

Instagram search reads the caption text, and the text on the image itself if there is any. If you write “children's haircuts in Zemun, Saturdays from 9:00”, the post can show up for people searching for “children's haircuts Zemun”, even without a hashtag. **Write in the words customers use** when they search, not in the internal names of your services.

## Hashtags on other networks

The rules aren't the same everywhere. These are rough guidelines for each network, for a local business:

| Network | How many hashtags | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Instagram | up to 5 | accurate, local and topical |
| Facebook | 0 to 1 | they don't help much, the text matters more |
| LinkedIn | 2 to 3 | profession and field, at the end of the text |
| TikTok | 3 to 5 | topic and niche, plus words in the caption |
| YouTube Shorts | 1 to 2 | #Shorts and the topic |
| Pinterest | no hashtags | keywords in the pin title and description |
| Google Business Profile | no hashtags | practical information |

You can see how the same post looks once it's adapted for seven networks on the [home page, in the networks section](/#networks).

## A branded hashtag: is it worth it?

It is when other people use it too, not just you. For example, customers who post photos of your product, or people who come to an event you organise. Then it becomes the place where their posts are collected. If you're the only one using it, it does no harm, but it doesn't bring much either. Ask customers to use it, for instance with a small giveaway or by printing it on the receipt.

## How do you check whether a hashtag works?

In a post's insights, Instagram shows where people came from: the home feed, your profile, search or Explore. If the share from search and hashtags is small, that doesn't mean you should drop them. It means the post got its reach another way, which is to be expected.

A more useful test is a comparison. For two months, use the same local hashtag on half your posts and leave it off the other half. If there's a difference in reach from search, it will show after about twenty posts. If there isn't, **don't waste time hunting for the perfect tags**. Put that time into the picture and the first line.

Record the results for each post in the same spreadsheet where you track your other numbers. What else is worth recording is explained in the article on [social media analytics](@analitika-drustvenih-mreza). You can also write hashtags into your [monthly content calendar](@plan-objava-za-drustvene-mreze), next to the topic, so you don't have to come up with them at the last minute.

## Where AI helps

Sova suggests hashtags for each post based on the topic, the brand's location from its profile and the network's rules, and it sticks to the limit. You see the suggestion before the post goes out and can change it like any other part of the text. If you run social media for several brands, this saves time, because you don't have to remember the local tags for every client. There's more on this in the article on [managing social media for multiple clients](@vodjenje-drustvenih-mreza-za-vise-klijenata).

For the bigger picture of your Instagram content, read the article on [content pillars](@stubovi-sadrzaja) as well, because pillars give your hashtags a logic too, grouped by topic.

## Frequently asked questions

### How many hashtags can I use on Instagram?

Five at most per post and per Reel. Instagram started introducing this limit in December 2025, gradually, for all accounts.

### Do hashtags increase the number of followers?

Rarely, and only a little. They can help Instagram sort new profiles into the right topic. Followers come from good posts that people share and save.

### Where do hashtags go, in the caption or in a comment?

In the caption, at the end of the text. That way they're part of the post from the first moment. The first comment has no real advantage.

### Should I use hashtags in English?

Only if some of your customers are in English-speaking countries too. For a local business in Serbia, hashtags in Serbian, with the name of your town, work better.

posts.title: 40 social media post ideas, by type of business
posts.seoTitle: 40 social media post ideas by type of business
posts.description: A list of 40 concrete post ideas for Instagram, Facebook and LinkedIn: for any business, cafés and restaurants, salons, shops and B2B services.
posts.excerpt: Concrete post ideas you can use this week, sorted by type of business, with an example for each group and a rule for spreading them across the month.
posts.body:
The best post ideas come from your everyday work: **customer questions, how your product is made, the people who work for you and the results you get for clients**. Below are 40 concrete ideas: ten for any business, plus seven or eight each for four types of business. Pick five, put them in next month's plan and get going.

:::ukratko
- The best source of ideas is the questions customers ask you every day.
- **Behind the scenes** posts and posts about your team almost always do better than advertising.
- Any idea can be a photo, a carousel, a short video or a story.
- Make sales posts one in three or four, not every post.
- Repeat ideas that did well after a few months, in a new format.
:::

## Ten ideas for any business

1. The answer to the question customers ask you most often.
2. What the morning before opening looks like.
3. Meet the team: one person, what they do and what they love about the job.
4. Before and after: the result of your work, with the customer's permission.
5. A customer's impression, copied from a message or review, with their permission.
6. A mistake customers often make and how to avoid it.
7. Something new on offer, with the price and how to order.
8. A number from your business: how many coffees a day, how many years you've been open, how many customers you've served.
9. A local recommendation: the shop next door, an event in town, a place you love.
10. A question for your audience: which of two new things should you introduce?

These ten cover all three basic content groups: your offer, the story behind the business and useful information. How to spread them across the month is explained in the article on [content pillars](@stubovi-sadrzaja).

!slika:ideje-za-objave-na-drustvenim-mrezama-info

## Cafés, restaurants and bakeries

1. How the dish of the day is made, in a 20-second video.
2. Who your baker or chef is and how long they've been with you.
3. The weekend menu, posted on Thursday.
4. Ingredient of the week: where it comes from and why you chose that one.
5. Your best-selling dish and why people order it.
6. The coffee you make differently from everyone else.
7. Holiday bookings, with the last date to book.
8. A local supplier: the farm, bakery or brewery you work with.

Food is the most rewarding subject to photograph, but only when the picture is good. Daylight by a window and a phone held overhead solve most problems. There's more on this in the article on [social media for restaurants and cafés](@drustvene-mreze-za-restorane-i-kafice).

## Salons, gyms, studios and clinics

1. Before and after, with a short explanation of what was done.
2. A myth from your profession and what the truth is.
3. Free slots for this week, in a story.
4. How to prepare for a first visit.
5. A piece of equipment or a product you use, and why.
6. A day in the life of a team member, from morning to closing time.
7. An expert's answer to a question from the comments.
8. A challenge for followers: seven days, one small habit.

With services, **people buy trust**. The face and name of the person who does the work, shown with their consent, build more trust than any graphic.

!slika:ideje-za-objave-na-drustvenim-mrezama-1

## Shops and online sales

1. The product in use, not just on a white background.
2. Three ways to combine a single product.
3. Opening a delivery of new stock.
4. How an order gets packed.
5. A comparison of two similar products and who each one suits.
6. The most common question about delivery and returns, answered clearly.
7. A photo a customer sent you, with their permission.

For online sales, **a short video of the product in someone's hand** works better than a studio photo, because it shows the size and the material. Ideas for clips are in the article on [Reels ideas for local businesses](@ideje-za-reels-za-lokalni-biznis).

## Services for companies (accountants, IT, agencies, consultants)

1. A deadline clients often forget and how not to miss it.
2. A case study: the problem, what you did, the result in numbers.
3. A change in regulations or tools, explained in five sentences.
4. What working with you looks like, step by step.
5. A question to ask before choosing a supplier in your field.
6. A lesson from a mistake, yours or someone else's, without naming the client.
7. A new team member and what they bring to clients.

These topics work best on LinkedIn, as a short story or a carousel. How to run a company page is covered in the article on [LinkedIn company pages](@linkedin-stranica-firme).

## How do you turn one idea into five posts?

One good idea isn't used up by a single post. Take “a mistake customers often make”:

- a carousel with five steps for avoiding it,
- a short video where you show the mistake and the fix,
- a story with a poll: “has this ever happened to you?”,
- a LinkedIn post with a story from your own work,
- an update on your Google Business Profile with a tip and a call to action.

That's five posts for two weeks, and only one idea. **Adapting for each network** is also the biggest part of the work that Sova takes over: from one topic it writes text that follows each network's rules and makes a visual in your brand colours. You can see how that looks on the [home page](/#networks).

## How do you spread ideas across the month?

A rule that works for most small businesses: out of every four posts, **one sells and three give something**. A tip, a story, something to smile at, a piece of information. People follow profiles they get something from, and those are the profiles they buy from, too.

Put your ideas in a monthly plan, alternate the types of post (photo, carousel, video) and leave room for whatever comes up along the way. The process is described in the article on [building a content calendar](@plan-objava-za-drustvene-mreze), and how many posts are enough is covered in the article on [how often to post](@koliko-cesto-objavljivati-na-drustvenim-mrezama).

## When ideas run dry

It will happen. When it does, one of these helps:

- Go through your messages and comments from the last three months and pull out the questions.
- Look at your three best posts from last year and make a new version of each.
- Ask someone on your team what customers ask them most often.
- Walk around your shop with your phone and photograph ten small details customers never see.

Sova can also suggest topics for the whole month, based on what it knows about your brand, your previous posts and their results. The suggestion always waits for your decision. You can start a trial [for free](/register).

## Frequently asked questions

### What should I post when I have no ideas?

The answer to a question a customer asked you this week. It's the safest topic, because you know someone is interested. If you don't even have that, show what your work looks like behind the scenes.

### How many sales posts is too many?

If every other post is an ad, that's too many. A good ratio is one sales post for every three or four that give something: a tip, a story or a piece of information.

### Can I repeat an old post?

You can, after a few months and in a new format. Most of your followers never saw the old post, and the ones who did will be glad to see it again if it was useful.

### Are trends and challenges good for a small business?

Sometimes. A trend that fits your business and your tone can bring you reach. A forced trend that has nothing to do with what you do usually brings a few likes and not a single customer.

posts.title: 20 Reels ideas for local businesses, shot on your phone
posts.seoTitle: 20 Reels ideas for local businesses
posts.description: Twenty short video ideas for cafés, salons, shops and services, plus how to shoot Reels on your phone: the first second, length, on-screen text and sound.
posts.excerpt: Short video is the quickest way to reach people who don't follow you yet. Twenty ideas you can shoot on your phone in a few minutes, plus the rules for the first second, length and sound.
posts.body:
For a local business, what works best is **short videos of 10 to 30 seconds that show a process, a result or the people behind the work**: how a coffee is made, before and after a haircut, an order being packed, the morning before opening. You shoot them on your phone, vertically, in daylight. Below are 20 ideas by type of business, and the rules that decide whether anyone keeps watching after the first second.

:::ukratko
- The first second decides everything: movement, a result or a question right at the start.
- **Ten to thirty seconds** is enough for most small business ideas.
- Shoot vertically (9:16), in daylight, with a steady hand or a tripod.
- On-screen text is a must, because many people watch with the sound off.
- The same video can go on Instagram, Facebook, TikTok and YouTube Shorts, with a caption adapted to each.
:::

## Why Reels, when you already have photos?

Reels are also shown to people who don't follow you. A photo in the feed mostly reaches your followers, while a short video has a chance of being seen by someone in your neighbourhood who has never heard of you. For a local business, it's the cheapest way to let new people know you exist.

The second reason is trust. Video shows things a photo can't: the sound of coffee being ground, the way a hairdresser moves, what the place looks like as you walk in. After that, a customer arrives feeling as if they've already been.

## The rules of a good video, in four points

!slika:ideje-za-reels-za-lokalni-biznis-info

**The first second needs movement or a result.** Don't open with a logo, a greeting or an empty shot. Start with the most interesting moment: the finished cake, the hair after the blow-dry, a full shop window.

The middle shows the process, quickly. Short shots of one to two seconds hold attention better than one long shot.

The end says what to do next: the address, “book by message”, “see you on Saturday”. Put it in on-screen text, not just in your voice.

**On-screen text carries the message even without sound.** Large letters, short sentences, kept away from the edges, where the app's buttons won't cover them.

## Ideas for cafés, restaurants and bakeries

1. The first croissants coming out of the oven, with the sound of the crunch.
2. Making a coffee from grinding to cup, in 15 seconds.
3. The dish of the day, from ingredients to plate.
4. What a chef eats after a shift.
5. The place before opening, empty, then full of guests.

## Ideas for salons, gyms and studios

6. Before and after, with a transition on a finger snap or a spin.
7. One exercise anyone can do at home, shown by a trainer.
8. A myth from your trade in three sentences, with the on-screen text “Myth:” and “Truth:”.
9. How the place gets ready for the first client of the morning.
10. A product you use and why, without advertising the brand.

!slika:ideje-za-reels-za-lokalni-biznis-1

## Ideas for shops and online sales

11. Packing one order, from the box to the tape.
12. Unboxing new stock.
13. Three ways to wear or use one product.
14. A product in your hand, from every angle, so people can see the size.
15. The question customers ask most often, answered in ten seconds.

## Ideas for services and companies

16. A day in the office or out on a job, in ten shots.
17. One tip from your field, said to camera, in 30 seconds or less.
18. What a first meeting with you looks like, step by step.
19. A new team member and what they do.
20. The result of a project: before, during, after.

Each of these ideas takes a few minutes to shoot, with no studio editing. There are more ideas for other types of post in the [list of 40 ideas](@ideje-za-objave-na-drustvenim-mrezama).

## How long should a Reel be?

Instagram allows longer videos too, but according to the available data, videos longer than three minutes aren't recommended to people who don't follow you. For a local business that's not a problem anyway: **most ideas need less than 30 seconds**. People are more likely to watch a shorter video to the end, and even several times, and that's a sign the content is good.

The rule is that a video lasts as long as the thing you're showing, sped up. Three minutes of making a coffee becomes 15 seconds.

## Sound and music

Business accounts on Instagram don't have access to all the music in the library, because some songs are licensed for personal accounts only. For a business account, the safe options are original sounds (the grinder, the oven, the scissors), your own voice and library music marked as available for businesses. A popular song from the internet, added to the video outside the app, can get the sound or the whole video removed.

Original sound has another advantage: nobody else has it. The crackle of a bread crust becomes your signature, and after a few videos people start to recognise it.

## Shooting on your phone: five tips

- Wipe the lens. It sounds silly, but half of all blurry videos are down to a finger on the glass.
- Shoot by a window, during the day. Daylight beats any lamp.
- Put your phone on a tripod or lean it against something. A steady picture looks professional.
- Shoot more short clips than you need, then pick the best ones.
- Shoot a whole week's material in one go, say on Monday morning.

Shooting in batches saves the most time. Once you've set up the tripod and the light, **five videos take as long as one**. Put them straight into your [content calendar](@plan-objava-za-drustvene-mreze), with a day and a topic, and during the week all you have to do is write the captions.

## One video, four networks

The same vertical video can go on Instagram Reels, Facebook Reels, TikTok and YouTube Shorts. What changes is the caption: shorter and more relaxed on TikTok, a title of up to 100 characters with the #Shorts tag on YouTube, and a caption with a call to action and up to five hashtags on Instagram. TikTok has its own article, [TikTok for business](@tiktok-za-firme), and hashtags are covered in the article on [Instagram hashtags](@hashtagovi-na-instagramu).

Sova publishes a video to all of these networks from one draft, with a caption adapted to each. When you don't have your own footage, it can suggest a video from Pexels for the post's topic, and it can turn a carousel into a short video made of the slides. Still, your own footage from the shop works better than any stock video. You can see how the same post looks on seven networks on the [home page](/#networks), and how video fits into a weekly rhythm in the article on [how often to post](@koliko-cesto-objavljivati-na-drustvenim-mrezama).

## Frequently asked questions

### How long should a Reel be for a small business?

Between 10 and 30 seconds for most ideas. According to the available data, videos longer than three minutes aren't recommended to people who don't follow you.

### Do I need professional equipment?

No. A phone, daylight and a tripod costing a few thousand dinars (RSD) are enough. The idea and the first second matter more than the camera.

### Can I use popular music?

On a business account, use only the music the app offers you as available for businesses, or original sound. A song added outside the app can get the sound or the video removed.

### Should I put the same video on TikTok too?

Yes, with an adapted caption and without another app's watermark. The networks don't like videos with a competitor's logo in the corner.

posts.title: Instagram carousels: how to make a post people swipe through to the end
posts.seoTitle: Instagram carousel posts: how to make one, with examples
posts.description: How to make an Instagram carousel people swipe through and save: the 4:5 format, the first slide, one idea per slide, slide count and six types for business.
posts.excerpt: A carousel is a post of several slides that people swipe through and save. How to build the first slide, how many slides to use and six types of carousel that work for a small business.
posts.body:
An Instagram carousel is a post with several photos or slides, **up to 20 in a single post**, that people swipe through. It works well for step-by-step tips, before and after shots, lists and short stories, because people save and share posts like these. The rule for success is simple: the first slide has to promise something, and every slide after it has to deliver part of that promise.

:::ukratko
- A carousel can have up to 20 slides, but five to ten is enough for most topics.
- The first slide works as a headline, so it carries **a promise, a question or a number**.
- One idea per slide, large text, the same design on every slide.
- The last slide says what to do next: save it, send a message, book.
- The 4:5 format (1080 by 1350 pixels) takes up the most screen space in the feed.
:::

## Why do carousels work so well?

A carousel holds attention longer than a single photo. Every swipe is a small decision to stay, and Instagram sees that people are spending time on the post. The second reason is usefulness: people save a carousel with five steps or ten tips so they can look at it later, and saves are one of the strongest signals that content is worth something.

For a small business, a carousel has a practical advantage too. You don't need a camera or any video editing. Good text and a simple design are enough, or a few photos from your shop arranged into a story.

## Format and technical rules

- The 4:5 format, or 1080 by 1350 pixels, takes up the most space on a phone screen.
- All the slides should be the same format. If you set the first one to 4:5, the rest adjust to it.
- You can use up to 20 slides per post, with photos, video or a mix of both.
- The text on a slide should be large enough to read on a phone without zooming. If you have to zoom in, the text is too small.

!slika:instagram-karusel-info

## How to build a carousel, slide by slide

Most good carousels follow the same layout:

1. A title slide with a promise: “5 mistakes that make your hair colour fade faster”.
2. The problem: why it matters, in one or two sentences.
3. The solution in steps: one step or tip per slide.
4. An example: a photo, a before and after, or a short customer story.
5. A call to action: what the reader should do next.

The first slide does the same job as the first sentence of a caption: it decides whether anyone swipes on. **Without a good first slide, the others might as well not exist.** The first sentence and the caption under the carousel are covered in the article on [how to write Instagram captions](@kako-napisati-opis-za-instagram-objavu).

## How many slides?

As many as the topic needs, not one more and not one fewer. A three-step tip is three slides plus a title and a call to action, five in total. A list of ten items is twelve slides. If a slide is only there to make the carousel longer, people sense it and give up halfway.

For most small business topics, **five to ten slides** is a good measure. Twenty makes sense for photo stories, for example a whole evening at an event or every haircut from one month.

## Six types of carousel for a small business

| Type | Example | Who it's for |
|---|---|---|
| Step-by-step tips | five steps to shiny hair after colouring | salons, clinics, specialists |
| Before and after | a renovated flat, a freshly done manicure, a cleaned car | services with a visible result |
| List | ten gifts under 2,000 dinars (RSD) | shops |
| Story | from flour to croissant in 36 hours | bakeries, craftspeople, producers |
| Case study | the client's problem, the solution, the result | services for businesses |
| Menu or price list | weekend menu, service prices | hospitality, salons |

For topic ideas there's also a [list of 40 post ideas](@ideje-za-objave-na-drustvenim-mrezama), and almost any of them can become a carousel.

!slika:instagram-karusel-1

## Design without a designer

You don't need a professional designer to make a good carousel. You need consistency:

- one or two fonts, always the same ones,
- two or three colours from your brand,
- the same position for the headline on every slide,
- a slide number or an arrow that tells people there's more,
- enough white space, because nobody reads a cluttered slide.

Once you've made a template, **every carousel after that is just new text**.

Check the carousel on your phone before you post it, not on a computer. What looks readable on a big screen is often tiny on a phone. If you can't read a slide in two seconds, cut the text or make the letters bigger. Watch the edges as well: Instagram sometimes crops part of the image in the feed, so keep important text away from the edges. Using the same template on every carousel builds recognition, and people know it's you in the feed before they even read your name.

## Carousels in Sova

Sova makes carousels in your brand's style. On the brand page you choose one of twenty-two styles for posts, carousels and stories, the format (4:5, 1:1 or 9:16), the colours and the number of slides. When you create a new post, Sova writes the slide text, the caption and the hashtags in one step, and draws the slides in the style you chose. It can take photos from your Gallery or from Unsplash and Pexels.

The draft goes for approval, where you swipe through the slides, change the text and schedule it. You can also turn a finished carousel into a short video, in 9:16 or 4:5, so the same topic goes out as a Reel too. For businesses that want something quick, with no writing, there are also ready-made templates you just fill in: a client testimonial, before and after, a price list, “we're hiring” and others. You can see how it looks in the [features section](/#features).

## Carousel or Reel?

You don't have to choose. **Reels bring in more new people** who don't follow you yet. Carousels bring more saves and closer reading from people who already follow you. A good plan has both, say one carousel and one Reel a week. Ideas for short videos are in the article on [Reels ideas for local businesses](@ideje-za-reels-za-lokalni-biznis), and how to spread everything across the month is in the article on [the content calendar](@plan-objava-za-drustvene-mreze).

Carousels work outside Instagram too. On LinkedIn, similar content is posted as a document, slide by slide, and it does well with professional topics. There's more on that in the article on [the LinkedIn company page](@linkedin-stranica-firme).

## Frequently asked questions

### How many slides can an Instagram carousel have?

Up to 20 photos or videos in one post. For most topics, five to ten is enough.

### Which format is best for a carousel?

Portrait 4:5, or 1080 by 1350 pixels. It takes up the most screen space in the feed, and all the slides should be the same format.

### Can a carousel include video?

Yes. A carousel can mix photos and videos. A video in first place grabs attention, but a title slide with a clear promise is often the safer choice.

### Is a carousel better than a Reel?

They do different jobs. Reels bring in new people, while carousels bring saves and trust among your existing followers. A combination of the two formats gives the best results.

posts.title: How to write an Instagram caption people read to the end
posts.seoTitle: How to write an Instagram caption, with examples
posts.description: How to write an Instagram caption: a first line that stops the scroll, specific text, a call to action and up to five hashtags. With before and after examples.
posts.excerpt: A good caption has four parts: a hook, specific content, a clear call to action and a few hashtags. Before and after examples for a bakery, a salon and an accountant.
posts.body:
A good Instagram caption has four parts: **a first line that stops the scroll, specific content, one clear call to action and up to five hashtags**. The first line matters most, because under the photo Instagram shows only the start of the text, and the rest sits behind “more”. If the opening doesn't catch people's interest, nobody will read the rest.

:::ukratko
- The first line does most of the work: a promise, a question or a surprising fact.
- Specific beats general, so write **a number, a time, a place and the name of a product**.
- One call to action per post, not three.
- Since December 2025, Instagram allows a maximum of five hashtags per post.
- A caption can be up to 2,200 characters long, but the length should follow the content.
:::

## Why does the first line matter so much?

On a phone screen, below the post you see the profile name and roughly the first two sentences of the caption. Everything else is hidden behind “more”. People decide whether to tap in less than a second, looking at the picture and that opening.

So the first line can't be “Good morning, dear followers!” or “New on the menu!”. It has to tell people why they should keep reading. Three forms that work well:

- a promise of something useful: “Three mistakes that make hair colour fade faster.”
- a question that hits home: “Do you know why homemade bread goes stale by the next day?”
- a surprising fact: “Each of our croissants takes 36 hours to make.”

## Four parts of a good caption

!slika:kako-napisati-opis-za-instagram-objavu-info

After the hook comes the content. The rule here is simple: **specific beats general**. “Quality products at affordable prices” means nothing, because everyone writes it. “Croissants made with French butter, 180 dinars, every morning from 7:00” tells you exactly what you get.

The third part is the call to action. One, clear, and with a way to do it: “Book an appointment by message”, “Save this post for your next trip to the shop”, “Tell us in the comments which colour you'd pick”. Three calls to action in the same post confuse the reader, so they end up doing nothing.

Hashtags go at the end. Since December 2025, Instagram has allowed **a maximum of five hashtags** per post and per Reel. That's a good thing, because it matters more that they're accurate than that there are lots of them. How to choose them is covered in the article on [Instagram hashtags](@hashtagovi-na-instagramu).

## Before and after examples

Three real types of post, rewritten using the rules above.

| Business | Before | After (first line) |
|---|---|---|
| Bakery | “Fresh bread every day! Come and visit us.” | “Yeast bread that keeps for three days without going rubbery.” |
| Hair salon | “New treatment available, ask us for details.” | “Hair dry after colouring? Here's what we're doing differently from 1 November.” |
| Accountant | “A reminder to our clients about deadlines.” | “The filing deadline is the 15th. Two things sole traders forget every single time.” |

You can see the pattern: a specific thing, a specific problem or a specific date. Anyone can write an opening like that, but you need to know what's bothering your customer.

!slika:kako-napisati-opis-za-instagram-objavu-1

## How long should a caption be?

Instagram allows up to 2,200 characters. That doesn't mean you should use them all. The length depends on the content:

- Short, one to three sentences, when the picture says it all: a new dish, a new haircut, a photo of your space.
- Medium, five to ten sentences, when you're explaining something: how to use a product, what a service includes.
- Long, when you're telling a story or giving advice in steps. Then split the text into short paragraphs with a blank line between them.

**Nobody reads a long block of text on a phone.** Short paragraphs, one thought each, are easy to read.

## Emojis: yes or no?

It depends on your tone. A café for students can use them more freely, a law firm more carefully. If you use them, let them replace or emphasise a word rather than sit at the end of every sentence. One to three per caption is usually enough. Your tone rules are worth writing down once, for all your posts. That's what the article on [brand voice](@glas-brenda-na-drustvenim-mrezama) is about.

## Words people search for

Instagram search reads the caption text too, not just the hashtags. If you're writing about children's haircuts in Zemun (a part of Belgrade), make sure the caption says “children's haircuts” and “Zemun”, naturally, in a sentence. That helps people looking for exactly that to find you. The same goes for posts about products: use the words your customers use, not your internal names.

## Captions for Reels, carousels and stories

With Reels, the caption matters less, because people are watching the video. The first line should confirm what the video promises, and the text on the video itself carries the message. With carousels, the caption says what's on the slides and why it's worth swiping to the end. With stories, the text is at its shortest: one sentence on the image itself and a sticker with a question, a poll or a link, because people only look at a story for a few seconds. The articles on [carousels](@instagram-karusel) and [Reels ideas](@ideje-za-reels-za-lokalni-biznis) cover carousels and Reels in detail.

## Checking before you post

Before you tap “Share”, read the caption out loud. If you stumble over a sentence, so will the reader. Then check four things. Does the first line give people a reason to tap “more”? Does the text contain at least one specific fact, number or name? Is there one clear call to action? Are the hashtags accurate?

Finally, look at the post through the eyes of a customer who doesn't know you. Do they know what you sell, where you are and how to contact you? **If they don't, add one sentence.** That's usually all that's missing for a post to bring in a message and not just a like.

You're allowed to edit a caption after posting. If you spot a mistake in a price or in your opening hours, fix it straight away, because wrong information does more harm than a correction.

## How does AI help with writing captions?

AI writes quickly and is good at adapting text to a network's rules. Its weakness is that it knows nothing about your business until you tell it. That's why general tools often produce text that sounds like an ad for anyone at all.

Sova first reads your website and builds a brand profile: services, prices, tone, audience, facts. Every caption it writes draws on that profile and on the brand voice you approved, so “Pekara Zrno” gets a caption about croissants at 7:00, not about “quality bakery products”. You always see the text before it goes out and can change whatever you like. You can see how it works in the [features section](/#features), and what AI can really do in the article on [AI for social media](@vestacka-inteligencija-za-drustvene-mreze).

## Frequently asked questions

### How many characters can an Instagram caption have?

Up to 2,200. The preview shows only the beginning, roughly the first two sentences, so put the most important part first.

### How many hashtags should I use?

Five at most, because that's the limit Instagram introduced in December 2025. Choose the ones that describe the post and the location accurately, not the most popular ones.

### Do hashtags go in the caption or in a comment?

In the caption. That way they're part of the post from the very first moment and search sees them straight away. Putting them in the first comment has no real advantage.

### Is a short caption better than a long one?

Neither is better in itself. Short when the picture says it all, longer when you're explaining something or telling a story. What matters is that the first line catches people's interest.

posts.title: How often to post on social media
posts.seoTitle: How often to post on social media
posts.description: How many posts a week on Instagram, Facebook, LinkedIn, TikTok and Google Business Profile: starting numbers and the rule that matters more.
posts.excerpt: Starting numbers for each network, why rhythm matters more than volume, and how to work out how many posts you can realistically keep up.
posts.body:
For a small business, a good start is **three posts a week on Instagram and Facebook, two on LinkedIn and one a week on Google Business Profile**. TikTok needs more, if you run it at all. What matters more than the exact number is keeping the rhythm going for months: three posts a week for half a year bring in more than daily posts for three weeks.

:::ukratko
- Rhythm matters more than numbers: choose what you can keep up for six months.
- **Three posts a week** is a good start for Instagram and Facebook.
- A LinkedIn company page works well with two posts a week, Google Business Profile with one.
- Short video (TikTok, Reels, Shorts) rewards posting more often.
- When you have nothing to say, it's better to skip a slot than to post filler.
:::

## Why does rhythm beat volume?

Social media algorithms track how people react to your posts. A profile that posts regularly gives them more data, and gives the audience a habit. When three weeks of daily posts are followed by a month of silence, people forget you, and your next post starts from zero.

The second reason is quality. When you try to post every day without a plan, after two weeks you start posting just anything. Weak posts don't only do badly on their own. They teach your audience to skip the next one.

## Starting numbers, by network

These are starting values for a small business with one person handling social media for a few hours a week. They aren't a rule. They're a point to start from, and then you measure.

!slika:koliko-cesto-objavljivati-na-drustvenim-mrezama-info

| Network | Posts a week | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Instagram | 3 posts and a few stories | stories can go up every day, short and informal |
| Facebook | 3 | same idea as on Instagram, different text |
| LinkedIn | 2 | on weekdays, in the morning |
| TikTok | 3 to 5 | short video, more is better as long as quality holds |
| YouTube Shorts | 2 to 3 | often the same video as the Reel, with a title for YouTube |
| Pinterest | 3 to 5 pins | a pin lives for months, so posting less often still pays off |
| Google Business Profile | 1 | an update, an offer or an event |

You don't have to be on every network. For most small businesses, two or three are enough. How to pick the right ones is explained in the [guide to social media management for small businesses](@vodjenje-drustvenih-mreza-za-mali-biznis).

## How do you work out what you can keep up?

Before you commit to a number, measure how long one post takes you from idea to publishing. For most people it's 30 to 60 minutes when they make posts one at a time, and 15 to 25 minutes when they work in batches.

An example: you have three hours a week. If one post takes 30 minutes, that's six posts a week, say three on Instagram and three on Facebook, with a little time left over for comments. If a post takes an hour, that's three posts, and then you're better off being on one network properly than on two by halves.

What saves the most time is a **monthly plan**, because you're no longer coming up with ideas every day. The process and a template are in the article on [building a content calendar](@plan-objava-za-drustvene-mreze).

!slika:koliko-cesto-objavljivati-na-drustvenim-mrezama-1

## Does posting more often lower the reach of each post?

Sometimes, yes. If you post three times on the same day, the posts compete with each other for the same audience. Spread them across the week. On TikTok and in Reels this is less of a problem, because every video gets its own chance with people who don't follow you.

A rule that works well: **one post a day on one network is the upper limit** for a small business on Instagram and Facebook. More than that only makes sense when you really do have a lot of good material, for example during a festival or an opening.

## When is it fine to skip a post?

When you have nothing to say. A “happy Monday” post without a picture from your work doesn't help anyone. It's better to skip the slot and next time post something people want to see.

To make sure this rarely happens, keep a list of ideas in reserve. We have a [list of 40 post ideas](@ideje-za-objave-na-drustvenim-mrezama) that covers most lines of business, and [content pillars](@stubovi-sadrzaja) help too, because every week then has its topics set in advance.

## Is there a penalty for a long break?

There's no rule under which a network punishes a profile for not posting for a month. But the effect is much like a penalty. The people who used to react to your posts have been reacting to other people's in the meantime, so the algorithm links them to other profiles. That's why the first post after a break usually does worse, and the second and third bring your old reach back.

If you know a break is coming, such as your annual holiday, **schedule posts in advance** for those two weeks. One post a week is enough to keep the profile alive.

## How often should you post Stories?

Stories last 24 hours, so people see them as something casual. For a local business they're a good place for small everyday things: what's on offer today, what the queue outside the door looks like, new stock. **Two to five stories a day** is perfectly normal, and you don't need them every day if you have nothing to show.

## What if you have several networks and little time?

Write one idea and adapt it for each network. The same news about a new service goes on Instagram with a photo and a longer caption, on Facebook with shorter text and an invitation to send you a message, and on LinkedIn as a story about why you introduced it. That's one idea and three posts.

Sova does exactly that. From one topic it writes text that follows each network's rules (length, hashtags, tone) and schedules the posts for slots that make sense. You choose how many posts a week you want, and Sova makes a plan that sticks to that number. You can see what one post adapted for seven networks looks like on the [home page, in the networks section](/#networks).

## How do you know if the number is right?

After two months, look at two things. Is the reach per post going up or down? Are messages and questions coming in? If reach is falling while you're posting more often, quality has probably dropped. If reach is rising and you have the time, add one more post a week. What else to track is covered in the article on [social media analytics](@analitika-drustvenih-mreza).

## Frequently asked questions

### How often should a small business post on Instagram?

Three posts a week and a few stories are a good start. If you keep that up for two months and have time for more, add a fourth post, ideally a short video.

### Is one post a week enough?

For Google Business Profile, yes. For Instagram and Facebook it's the minimum that keeps a profile alive, but it rarely brings growth. If you can only manage one, make it a good one and post it regularly.

### Should I post at weekends?

If your customers are active at weekends, yes. For restaurants, cafés and shops, the weekend often brings more reactions. Services for companies can skip the weekend without losing anything.

### Which is better, more short posts or fewer longer ones?

It depends on the network. On TikTok and in Reels, more short videos usually work better. On LinkedIn and Facebook, one post with real substance is worth more than three empty ones.

posts.title: LinkedIn company page: how to set it up and what to post
posts.seoTitle: LinkedIn company page: setup and what to post
posts.description: How to set up a LinkedIn company page, what to post, how often, and how employees can help your reach. A guide for small firms and B2B services.
posts.excerpt: LinkedIn is the network where owners and managers make the decisions. How to set up a company page, five types of post that work, and why your employees are your biggest reach.
posts.body:
A LinkedIn company page makes sense when **your customers are other companies or the people who make decisions inside them**: owners, directors, procurement managers, HR. For businesses like these, two posts a week (case studies, professional tips and stories about the team) bring in more enquiries than any other network. The biggest reach, though, doesn't come from the page itself. It comes from employees who share the posts and comment on them.

:::ukratko
- LinkedIn is for services sold to companies, for hiring and for professional reputation.
- **Two posts a week**, on weekdays, are enough to start with.
- A case study with numbers is the strongest type of post for services.
- The personal profiles of owners and employees reach more people than the company page.
- A more serious tone, but the same brand voice as on your other networks.
:::

## Who really needs LinkedIn?

LinkedIn isn't for everyone. It will bring few customers to a café, a bakery or a hair salon, because people don't go there to pick a place for breakfast. But if you sell accounting, IT services, marketing, legal advice, equipment for companies or training, or if you're hiring, LinkedIn is where the decision makers are, and they're there while they're thinking about work.

The second reason to be on LinkedIn is recruitment. Candidates check out a company before the interview. A page with regular posts about the team and its projects tells them more than a job ad does.

## How to set up the page

Sort out the basics before your first post. People who land on the page decide within a few seconds whether you're serious.

1. A logo and a cover image in good quality, in your brand colours.
2. A short tagline under the name, in one sentence: what you do and for whom.
3. An About section with the words people search for: services, city, industry.
4. Website address, location, company size and sector.
5. A call-to-action button, for example a visit to your website or a contact link.
6. Connect your employees: ask them to list the company on their profiles, so the page shows up there too.

If you need a one-sentence description, use the same one you wrote down for your [brand voice](@glas-brenda-na-drustvenim-mrezama). The same sentence on your website, Instagram and LinkedIn makes you easier to recognise.

!slika:linkedin-stranica-firme-info

## Five types of post that work

**A case study is the strongest format for services.** The client's problem, what you did, the result in numbers. “We cut order processing time for a client in Kragujevac from three days to one.” Leave out the client's name if you don't have permission to use it.

A professional tip shows that you know your trade. A deadline companies forget, a mistake in a contract, a change in regulations explained in five sentences.

Team and culture posts show the people. A new colleague, a work anniversary, what a working day looks like. Posts like these often get the most reactions, because people react to people.

Company news: a new product, a new office, a certificate, an award. Keep it short and say why it matters to customers.

A document, meaning a carousel in PDF form, slide by slide. It works well for step-by-step tips and short guides. It's the same principle as an Instagram carousel, which is covered in the article on [carousel posts](@instagram-karusel).

## How often and when?

For a small company's page, **two posts a week** on weekdays is a good start. People scroll LinkedIn most in the morning, before and at the start of the working day, and around lunchtime. At weekends the network is quieter. As with any network, the page statistics after a month will show what holds true for your audience.

Consistency matters more than volume. Two posts a week over a whole year build a reputation. Five posts in one week followed by three months of silence build nothing. There's more about rhythm in the article on [how often to post](@koliko-cesto-objavljivati-na-drustvenim-mrezama).

!slika:linkedin-stranica-firme-1

## Your employees are your biggest reach

On LinkedIn, **personal profiles usually reach far more people** than company pages. **People trust a person more than a logo.** So the best strategy for a small company is a combination: the page posts, and the owner and employees share the post with a sentence of their own, or write their own posts about their work.

Don't force anyone. Ask two or three people who enjoy it. Give them a topic and the freedom to write in their own words. One honest comment from a colleague is worth more than ten identical shares.

## Tone on LinkedIn

LinkedIn calls for a more serious tone than Instagram, but that doesn't mean corporate language. Nobody reads “end-to-end solutions for process optimisation”. Everyone reads “We help companies process orders in one day instead of three”. Write the way you'd talk to a client in a meeting: clearly, specifically, without inflated words.

**The first two lines matter most**, because LinkedIn hides the rest of the text behind “more”.
