It's the same rule as for Instagram captions, covered in the article on [how to write Instagram captions](@kako-napisati-opis-za-instagram-objavu). Finish with two or three hashtags for your profession and sector.

## Links in posts

Many people who run LinkedIn pages notice that posts with a link to an external website do worse than posts without one, because the network wants people to stay on it. That's why a common practice is to write the text so it has value without a click, and to put the link in the first comment. LinkedIn hasn't officially confirmed this as a rule, so test it on your own page.

## How do you know LinkedIn is working?

Likes on LinkedIn say little. Look at three things: who reacts (are they people from the companies you sell to?), how many messages and enquiries come in after your posts, and how many people visit your page and your website. One enquiry from the right director is worth more than a hundred likes from people in your own trade. The page statistics also show which companies and sectors your visitors come from, which helps you see whether you're reaching the right audience. The other numbers worth tracking are described in the article on [social media analytics](@analitika-drustvenih-mreza).

## LinkedIn in Sova

Sova publishes to LinkedIn, both to a personal profile and to a company page, with text, an image or a video, and it can add a first comment. The text is written in a more serious tone than for Instagram, but from the same brand profile and in the same voice. One topic gets three versions: for Instagram, Facebook and LinkedIn.

Because of LinkedIn's rules, Sova doesn't publish there entirely on its own: even when Autopilot is on, you confirm LinkedIn posts yourself. You can see what one post looks like when it's adapted for each network on the [home page](/#networks). If you run LinkedIn for clients, read the article on [managing social media for multiple clients](@vodjenje-drustvenih-mreza-za-vise-klijenata), and you can start a trial [for free](/register).

## Frequently asked questions

### Does a small company need a LinkedIn page?

If your customers are other companies or you're hiring, yes. If you sell to consumers, like a café or a salon, LinkedIn isn't a priority. Your time is better spent on Instagram and your Google Business Profile.

### Which is better, a personal profile or a company page?

Both, together. The page gives you credibility and a place for information, while the personal profiles of the owner and employees bring reach and trust.

### How often should I post on a LinkedIn page?

Two posts a week, on weekdays, is a good start. Keeping the rhythm going for months matters more than posting every day.

### Should I put the link in the post or in a comment?

Many people notice that posts without an external link do better, so they put the link in the first comment. LinkedIn hasn't officially confirmed this, so compare both approaches on your own page.

posts.title: The best time to post on Instagram: how to find yours
posts.seoTitle: The best time to post on Instagram in Serbia
posts.description: There's no single best time to post on Instagram. Here are good slots to start with, and how to find your own audience's time in four weeks.
posts.excerpt: General tables of the best times to post work for an average audience, and yours isn't average. Here are slots to start with, plus a four-week test that gives you the real answer.
posts.body:
The best time to post on Instagram is **the moment your audience is on their phones**, and for most local businesses in Serbia that means the morning before work (7:00 to 9:00), the lunch break (12:00 to 14:00) and the evening (19:00 to 21:00). Those slots are only a starting assumption. The real answer comes from your profile's insights and a simple four-week test.

:::ukratko
- There is no universal best time, only good starting assumptions.
- **Profile insights** show the days and hours when your followers are active.
- The test takes four weeks: the same type of post in two different slots, then a comparison of reach.
- Timing matters in the first hours after posting, but a weak post doesn't become good because of a good slot.
- Scheduling solves the problem when the best slot falls during your working hours.
:::

## Why does posting time matter at all?

Instagram doesn't show posts strictly in order, but the first hours after posting matter. If a post gets reactions straight away from the people who see it, it gets shown to a wider audience more often. If you post at 3 in the morning, when your followers are asleep, the first reactions only arrive hours later, and by then there are already a hundred newer posts ahead of it.

So timing doesn't create success, but it can slow it down. A good post in a bad slot does worse than it could. A weak post in a perfect slot stays weak.

## Good slots to start with

If you're just setting up your profile, or you don't have enough followers for insights yet, start from your audience's habits. These are starting assumptions for typical local businesses in Serbia, in Belgrade time:

| Type of business | Slots to try | Why then |
|---|---|---|
| Café, bakery, breakfast | 7:00 to 8:30 | people are choosing where to go for coffee or breakfast |
| Restaurant, food delivery | 11:30 to 12:30 and 18:00 to 19:30 | before lunch and before dinner |
| Salon, gym, studio | 19:00 to 21:00 | after work, when people plan their week |
| Clothes shop, gift shop | 20:00 to 22:00 | relaxed scrolling in the evening |
| Services for companies | 8:00 to 10:00 on weekdays | the start of the working day |

The weekend is a story of its own. On Saturday mornings the audience is usually slower and more relaxed, and on Sunday evenings activity picks up because people are planning the week ahead. For businesses linked to nights out, Friday afternoon often works better than Monday.

!slika:najbolje-vreme-za-objavu-na-instagramu-1

## Where can you see when your followers are active?

If you have a professional account (business or creator), Instagram shows you insights. In the section with follower insights there's an overview of the **most active times**: by day of the week and by hour. A minimum number of followers is needed before the overview appears, so small profiles sometimes don't see it.

There are two things to know before you trust those numbers. First, they're shown in the time zone the app uses, so check that it's Belgrade time. Second, the most active time is also the most crowded time, because that's when everyone posts. Sometimes a post an hour earlier, before the peak, does better.

## The four-week test

Insights tell you when people are online. **The test tells you when they react to your posts**, and that's what you actually want to know. The process is simple:

!slika:najbolje-vreme-za-objavu-na-instagramu-info

1. Pick two slots, for example Tuesday at 8:00 and Tuesday at 20:00.
2. For four weeks, post the same type of content in both slots. Compare a carousel with a carousel, a Reel with a Reel.
3. After 48 hours, write down the reach and the number of saves and shares.
4. After four weeks, compare the averages. A slot that does more than 20% better becomes your slot.

Why 48 hours? Because by then most of the reach has already come in, and it's still early enough to measure every post by the same yardstick. Other metrics worth tracking are described in the article on [social media analytics](@analitika-drustvenih-mreza).

## Is it different for Reels?

Partly. Reels keep being shown to people who don't follow you for longer, so the first hours carry a little less weight than with a regular post. Early reactions still help, though, so don't post a Reel while your audience is asleep. For short video ideas, see the article on [Reels ideas for local businesses](@ideje-za-reels-za-lokalni-biznis).

With Stories, timing matters more, because a story lasts 24 hours and people watch it when they open the app. A morning story catches people on their way to work, an evening one catches the people scrolling before bed.

## What if the best slot is while you're working?

That's the most common problem for small businesses. The best time to post is exactly when the shop is full. The solution is **scheduling**: you make the post when you have some peace and quiet, and it goes out on its own at the time you set. How to do this in Meta's tools and in other apps is covered in the article on [scheduling posts on Instagram and Facebook](@zakazivanje-objava-na-instagramu-i-facebooku).

Sova schedules posts in the brand's time zone, even when you change the zone or the clocks go forward or back. Once the profile has enough posts with results, it suggests slots based on your account's history, and before that, on assumptions for your type of business. You can see what the calendar with scheduled posts looks like on the [home page](/#features).

## How often should you post, now that you know when?

A good slot without a rhythm doesn't help. If you post once every two weeks at the perfect time, the result will still be weak, because people forget about you between posts. For a local business, a good start is **three posts a week** and a few stories. The details are in the article on [how often to post](@koliko-cesto-objavljivati-na-drustvenim-mrezama), and you can lay out the whole month by following the guide in the article on [building a content calendar](@plan-objava-za-drustvene-mreze).

## The most common mistakes

- Posting whenever you get round to it, with no order at all, so you have nothing to compare.
- Trusting generic tables from the internet that were made for an American audience in a different time zone.
- Changing the slot, the type of post and the topic all at once, so you don't know what made the difference.
- Deleting a post that got off to a slow start and posting it again, which usually doesn't help.

## Frequently asked questions

### What's the best time to post on Instagram in Serbia?

For most local businesses, good starting slots are 7:00 to 9:00 in the morning, 12:00 to 14:00 and 19:00 to 21:00, Belgrade time. The right time for your profile comes from the most active times in your insights and from the four-week test.

### Is the weekend a good time to post?

It depends on the business. For restaurants, cafés and nightlife, the weekend is often the best part of the week. For services for companies, weekdays work better. Check your insights to see when your followers are active.

### Should I post at the same time every day?

It doesn't have to be the same time, but regular slots help both you and your audience. When followers know that a new offer goes up every Tuesday morning, they go looking for it themselves.

### Does a scheduled post do worse than one posted by hand?

There's no reliable evidence that Instagram penalises scheduled posts made through official tools. What matters is that the post is good and that you reply to comments in the first few hours.

posts.title: Social media content calendar: how to plan a whole month in an hour
posts.seoTitle: Social media content calendar: a month in an hour
posts.description: How to make a monthly social media content calendar: the columns you need, five steps, an example week and the most common calendar mistakes.
posts.excerpt: A monthly content plan saves more time than any trick. Five steps, the columns you actually need and an example week for a hair salon.
posts.body:
A content calendar is **a table that gives the date, network, type of post, topic and call to action for every slot in the month**. You make it once a month, in an hour or two, and after that every post takes half as long, because you're not coming up with an idea on the spot. You don't need any special software to start: a spreadsheet or a notebook is enough.

:::ukratko
- Make the plan once a month, not every morning.
- **Seven columns** are enough: date and time, network, type, topic, pillar, call to action, status.
- Put in the month's important dates first, and only then the regular posts.
- Leave one or two free slots a week for whatever comes up along the way.
- The plan isn't set in stone: if something important happens, move a post.
:::

## Why does a plan save so much time?

Without a plan, every post starts with the question “what do I post today?”. That question takes more time than the writing itself. On top of that, when you come up with something in a hurry, you usually post the same thing as last week, and the profile becomes monotonous.

With a plan, you work in batches. You decide on topics once, shoot once, write once. Your brain isn't constantly jumping between tasks, so everything goes faster.

## Which columns does the plan need?

Many templates on the internet have twenty columns. Most small businesses need seven:

| Column | What you enter | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Date and time | when it goes out | Tuesday 3 November at 19:00 |
| Network | where it goes out | Instagram |
| Type | the format of the post | carousel, Reel, photo, story |
| Topic | what it's about, in one sentence | five haircuts for short hair |
| Pillar | which group of topics it belongs to | tips |
| Call to action | what you want people to do | book an appointment by message |
| Status | how far you've got | idea, written, scheduled |

The “pillar” column shows you whether your content is balanced, so that it isn't all selling. What pillars are and how to set them is covered in the article on [content pillars](@stubovi-sadrzaja).

## Five steps to a monthly plan

!slika:plan-objava-za-drustvene-mreze-info

1. Write down the month's goal in one sentence. For example, “ten new clients for keratin treatment” or “people should know we're open on Sundays too”.
2. Put in the important dates: holidays, promotions, seasonal events, anniversaries, new products. They get their slots first.
3. Set the schedule: how many posts a week, on which networks and on which days. If you don't know how many is enough, see the article on [how often to post](@koliko-cesto-objavljivati-na-drustvenim-mrezama).
4. For each slot, write the topic in one sentence. Alternate the pillars and the types of post.
5. Write the captions in one or two sittings and **schedule them straight away**.

Once you get used to it, the first four steps take **an hour**. The fifth step takes longer, but you can spread it across the weeks.

## Where do you get topics when you have none?

The best source is your customers' questions. Anything people ask you at the till, on the phone or in messages is a topic for a post, because you know someone is interested in it. Keep a note on your phone and add questions as they come in. After a month you'll have more topics than slots.

The second source is your best old posts. Something that did well six months ago can go out again, with a new photo and slightly different text. The third source is the season: what people in your line of business look for in November, and what they look for in May. **A bakery in December** talks about slava cakes (slava is the family saint's day that many Serbian families celebrate) and gift boxes, and in June about cold drinks and breakfast outdoors.

## An example week for a hair salon

A salon in Novi Sad, on Instagram and Facebook, three posts a week plus stories. The month's goal: fill the appointments on Tuesdays and Wednesdays, when it's quietest.

| Day | Network | Type | Topic | Call to action |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Monday 19:00 | Instagram and Facebook | carousel | five hairstyles that last until your next cut | save it for next time |
| Wednesday 12:00 | Instagram | Reel | 30 seconds of before and after, colouring | book an appointment by message |
| Friday 18:00 | Instagram and Facebook | photo | Milica, the new hairdresser on the team | welcome her in the comments |
| Every day | Instagram | stories | free appointments for today | send us a message |

Notice how tips, work and people take turns. **There is a sales call, but it isn't in every post.** You'll find more ideas for each line of business in the [list of 40 post ideas](@ideje-za-objave-na-drustvenim-mrezama).

!slika:plan-objava-za-drustvene-mreze-1

## Where should you keep the plan?

For one person, a spreadsheet in Excel or Google Sheets is enough. For a team of two or three, a shared calendar is useful, so everyone can see what's scheduled and who's doing what.

The problem with a spreadsheet is that it doesn't publish anything. You still have to copy every post into the network or into a scheduling tool, and that's where half the saving gets lost. Scheduling options are described in the article on [scheduling posts on Instagram and Facebook](@zakazivanje-objava-na-instagramu-i-facebooku).

## How does Sova make a monthly plan?

In Sova, the plan takes one click, for one month or for up to three months ahead. You choose the month, the number of posts a week, the networks and the types of post, and you can add a note, such as “push gift vouchers in December”. Sova spreads the slots across the best hours and suggests a topic, a goal and a call to action for each slot, based on what it knows about your brand from your website.

You remove the topics you don't like, change dates if you need to and press “Generate all”. Each post becomes a draft with text and a visual, waiting for your approval. You can see what that flow looks like on the [home page](/#how). You can try the plans [for free](/register).

## The most common mistakes in a plan

- A plan with no goal for the month, so the posts look nice but lead nowhere.
- Only sales posts. People follow profiles that give them something, not ones that only sell.
- Too many posts in the plan. It's better to plan nine posts you'll actually publish than twenty, half of which never go out.
- No free slots. When something nice happens in the shop, there's nowhere to put it.
- Nobody looks at the plan once the month is over. At the end of the month, check which topics did best and repeat them. How to do that is covered in the article on [analytics](@analitika-drustvenih-mreza).

## Frequently asked questions

### How far ahead should you make a content calendar?

A month ahead is a good measure for most small businesses. For seasonal work, before the holidays for example, it helps to have a rough plan for two to three months and to work out the details a month before it starts.

### Does the plan have to be the same for every network?

No. The same topic can go on several networks, but the type of post, the text and the timing are adapted. On LinkedIn a story works better, on Instagram a carousel or a short video.

### What if something important happens in the middle of the month?

Move the planned post and publish the news. That's why it's a good idea to leave one or two free slots a week in your plan.

### Can AI make a content calendar?

It can make a good suggestion, especially when it knows your brand, your offer and your tone. The final choice of topics and dates should stay with you, because only you know what's really going to happen in the shop next month.

posts.title: Content pillars: the three to five topics that carry your social media
posts.seoTitle: Content pillars: what they are and how to choose them
posts.description: What content pillars are, how to choose three to five topics and spread them across the month. Examples for a bakery, a salon, a shop and an IT company.
posts.excerpt: Content pillars are the recurring topics you post about. How to choose them from your goals and your customers' questions, examples for four types of business and how to use them in your plan.
posts.body:
Content pillars are **the three to five recurring topics your business posts about**, for example products, behind the scenes, tips and special offers. Every post belongs to one pillar. That way you plan faster, your profile doesn't turn into nothing but advertising, and at the end of the month you can see which topic brings in the most reactions and messages.

:::ukratko
- Three to five pillars are enough. Any more and your content gets spread too thin.
- Pillars come from two sources: **what you want to sell** and what customers want to know.
- Keep the sales pillar to a quarter of your posts at most.
- Any pillar can be a photo, a carousel, a video or a story.
- Measure results by pillar, not just by post.
:::

## Why do you need pillars?

Without pillars, every post is a new decision. A special offer today, holiday greetings tomorrow, another offer the day after. After two months the profile looks like a flyer, and people stop looking.

With pillars you have a framework. When you make your plan, you don't ask yourself “what should I post?” but “which pillar is up next, and what's the new topic within it?”. That's a much easier question. What a full monthly plan looks like is explained in the article on [building a content calendar](@plan-objava-za-drustvene-mreze).

## How do you choose your pillars?

Start with two lists.

The first list: what you want to achieve. More bookings on Tuesdays? Sales of a new service? People knowing that you deliver? Each goal suggests a topic.

The second list: what customers ask you. Write down the ten questions you hear most often. They usually fall into two or three topics, and those are your useful pillars.

Then bring the two lists together. A pillar has to meet at least one condition: it helps your goal or it answers a real customer need. The best pillars meet both.

!slika:stubovi-sadrzaja-info

## Example pillars for four types of business

| Business | Pillars |
|---|---|
| Bakery | products, behind the scenes (how it's made), tips and recipes, offers and holidays |
| Hair salon | before and after, hair care at home, the team, free slots |
| Clothing shop | new stock, how to put outfits together, customers wearing our clothes, offers |
| IT company | case studies, tips for business owners, team and culture, industry news |

Notice that in each example **at most one pillar sells directly**: offers or free slots. The product pillars show what's on offer, and the others build trust, show expertise or show the people behind the business. Whether a sales post works depends on exactly those posts.

## How many posts per pillar?

A simple starting split for four pillars:

- useful content (tips, answers): about 30%,
- product or service: about 30%,
- behind the scenes and people: about 25%,
- offers and sales calls to action: about 15%.

If you post three times a week, that's roughly twelve posts a month: four tips, four about the product, three behind the scenes and one or two offers. These numbers aren't set in stone. After two months, look at the results and shift the percentages towards the pillar that works best.

!slika:stubovi-sadrzaja-1

## A pillar is not a post format

A common mix-up: “Reels” isn't a pillar, and neither is “carousel”. A pillar is a topic, and the format is the way you show it. The pillar “hair care at home” can be a five-step carousel, a short video, a story with a poll or a post with a product photo. Alternate formats within a pillar, and your profile stays varied. Formats are covered in the articles on [carousels](@instagram-karusel) and [Reels ideas](@ideje-za-reels-za-lokalni-biznis).

## Campaigns: temporary pillars

Alongside your permanent pillars there are campaigns, topics with a start and an end. Opening a new location, a holiday offer, a new product. A campaign runs for a few weeks and during that time takes some of your slots, say one post a week. When it ends, the slots go back to the permanent pillars.

A campaign still has to respect the balance between selling and useful content. A month in which every post says “buy a gift voucher” wears your audience out before the holidays even arrive.

## The most common mistakes with pillars

The first mistake is having too many pillars. With eight of them, each gets one post a month and none of them makes an impression. People remember a business for two or three things, not eight. If you can't decide, merge similar ones: “tips” and “frequently asked questions” are usually the same pillar.

The second mistake is pillars that are really one pillar. If a clothing shop has the pillars “new stock”, “sale” and “offers”, all three say the same thing: buy. The profile then looks like a catalogue. **At least one pillar has to be about people**, and at least one about something useful for the customer that isn't your product.

The third mistake is a pillar you can't keep up. “Recipe of the week” sounds great, but if you don't have time to cook and take photos every week, the pillar disappears after a month. **Choose topics where the material already exists** in your everyday work, because then the posts practically make themselves.

The fourth mistake is writing the pillars down and forgetting about them. Put them in a column of your plan, next to each post, and you'll see at a glance whether the month is balanced or there are three offers in a row. **A pillar in your plan works, a pillar in a drawer doesn't.**

## How do you measure pillars?

At the end of the month, add up the results by pillar, not just by post: average reach, saves and shares, messages. You'll often find that one pillar keeps winning, for example “behind the scenes”. That's a signal to give it more room. Replace a pillar that brings in nothing three months in a row with a new one. What exactly to measure is covered in the article on [social media analytics](@analitika-drustvenih-mreza).

## How does Sova use pillars?

When Sova builds a strategy for your brand, it suggests pillars and campaigns based on what it has read on your website: your services, audience and goals. You can change, add or delete pillars. Every draft post has its own pillar, so the Monthly plan keeps the schedule balanced and Analytics shows results by pillar. When you switch on Autopilot, the weekly drafts follow the same pillar schedule and the rules you've set.

You can see what a strategy with pillars and a schedule looks like on the [home page](/#how). If you're just starting out, read the [guide to social media management for small business](@vodjenje-drustvenih-mreza-za-mali-biznis) as well, and for specific topics within each pillar, the [list of 40 post ideas](@ideje-za-objave-na-drustvenim-mrezama).

## Frequently asked questions

### What are content pillars?

The recurring topics a business posts about on social media, usually three to five. Every post belongs to one pillar, which makes planning and measuring easier.

### How many pillars should I have?

Three to five. With fewer than three your profile gets monotonous, and with more than five it's hard to post regularly in each one.

### Do pillars have to be the same on every network?

No, but they're usually similar. On LinkedIn the expertise pillar may take the lead, and on Instagram the behind the scenes one. What matters is that the brand's personality stays the same.

### How often should I change my pillars?

Rarely. Review them every three months and replace the one that keeps doing poorly. Pillars are the foundation, so you don't change them every month.

posts.title: TikTok for business: do you need it, and how to start without dancing
posts.seoTitle: TikTok for business: how to get started, step by step
posts.description: Whether TikTok suits your business, how to open a business account, what to film, how often to post and why you don't have to dance. A small business guide.
posts.excerpt: TikTok isn't just for teenagers and dance routines. How to judge whether it's right for you, what to film, how often to post and how to use one video on four networks.
posts.body:
TikTok makes sense for a business when **your product or service can be shown in a short video**: how it's made, how it's used, what the result looks like. You don't have to dance or follow every trend. To start, all you need is a business account, three videos a week shot on your phone and two to three months of patience.

:::ukratko
- TikTok also shows videos to people who don't follow you, so it's good for finding new customers.
- **A natural video shot on a phone** often does better than a polished ad.
- Three to five videos a week is a good rhythm to start with.
- A business account comes with analytics, but a limited choice of music.
- The same video can go on Reels and YouTube Shorts, with a different caption.
:::

## Is TikTok right for your business?

Ask yourself three questions. Can people see what you do? A bakery, a salon, a workshop, a shop, a gym and a restaurant all have something to show. Do your customers watch short videos? These days people in their 40s and 50s do too, not just the young. Do you have someone who will film three times a week? Without that, even the best idea won't help.

If the answers are yes, yes and yes, TikTok is worth a try. If you sell complex services to businesses, such as bookkeeping or software, LinkedIn is usually the better first choice. It's covered in the article on [the LinkedIn company page](@linkedin-stranica-firme).

## How does TikTok decide who sees your video?

TikTok first shows every new video to a small group of people, then watches how they react: do they watch to the end, do they watch it again, do they comment, share and save? If they react well, it shows the video to a bigger group. That's why even a profile with zero followers can have a video with thousands of views.

For a business, this means two things. First, **every video is a new opportunity**, however many followers you have. Second, **the first second and keeping people watching to the end** matter more than anything else.

!slika:tiktok-za-firme-info

## First steps

1. Open an account and switch it to a business account in the settings. You get analytics and the option of a link on your profile.
2. Write a short bio: what you do, where, and one call to action (“orders by message”).
3. Before your first post, watch twenty or so videos from similar businesses to get a feel for the rhythm and tone.
4. Film five videos in advance, then post three a week. Having a reserve stops you from going quiet.
5. After a month, look at your analytics to see which videos held people's attention longest.

## What should you film?

The videos that do best look as if a person filmed them, not an advertising agency:

- the process, from raw materials to finished product, sped up,
- before and after,
- an answer to a question from the comments, said to camera,
- a day in the shop, in ten short shots,
- a mistake customers make and how to avoid it,
- packing an order or getting ready to open.

Twenty more ideas, sorted by type of business, are in the article on [Reels ideas for local businesses](@ideje-za-reels-za-lokalni-biznis). They all work on TikTok too.

## TikTok without dancing and without your face

You don't have to appear on camera if you don't want to. Many successful business profiles show only hands and the product, or the space, with on-screen text and original sound. The sound of a coffee grinder, a pair of scissors or an oven is interesting enough.

Still, a face and a voice build trust faster. If someone on your team likes to talk, let them be the voice of the profile. **People follow people**, not logos.

Agree on just one thing: who films and who replies to comments. If that's two different people, make sure they keep each other in the loop. Customers notice when a question under a video sits for days without an answer, and TikTok notices when the conversation under a video is alive.

!slika:tiktok-za-firme-1

## How often should you post?

To start with, **three to five videos a week**. TikTok rewards regularity and gives every video a fresh chance, so posting more often usually brings more views, as long as the quality holds up. One good video is worth more than three rushed ones. How to set a rhythm you can keep up is covered in the article on [how often to post](@koliko-cesto-objavljivati-na-drustvenim-mrezama).

## Captions, hashtags and sound

A TikTok caption can be long, but a short one works better: one sentence that adds to the video, plus three to five hashtags, at least one of them with your location. TikTok search reads the caption, the on-screen text and what's said in the video, so use the words people type when they're searching: “custom cake Novi Sad”, not just the name of your cake.

Business accounts have access to a limited library of music cleared for commercial use. Popular songs that personal accounts use are often not available. That's not a big problem, because original sound and your own voice work very well.

## Common mistakes businesses make on TikTok

- Reposting an ad from television or Facebook. People skip a video that looks like an ad within the first second.
- A logo at the start. The first second has to show something interesting, not your logo.
- Videos with another app's watermark. The networks show them to fewer people.
- Giving up after two weeks. TikTok takes time, and the first few months are a learning period for you and for your audience.
- Ignoring comments. Your reply to a comment can be your next video.

## One video, four networks

A vertical video made for TikTok can also go on Instagram Reels, Facebook Reels and YouTube Shorts. Film it without a watermark and adapt the caption to each network. That way, one hour of filming a week covers four networks.

Sova does that adapting for you: from one topic it writes captions for TikTok, Instagram, Facebook and YouTube according to each network's rules, and puts the posts into the same calendar. On TikTok, because of that network's rules, Sova doesn't publish entirely on its own, and you confirm the post yourself. You can see how the same post looks on seven networks on the [home page](/#networks), and you can start a trial [for free](/register).

For the bigger picture on which networks to choose, read the [guide to social media management for small businesses](@vodjenje-drustvenih-mreza-za-mali-biznis).

## Frequently asked questions

### Is TikTok only for young people?

No. Every generation watches short videos these days, and TikTok shows each video to people who might like it. For a local business, that includes people in your own town.

### Do I have to appear in the videos?

No. Hands, the product, the space and on-screen text are enough. A face and a voice do build trust faster, though, so if someone on your team likes being on camera, make use of it.

### How long does it take to see results on TikTok?

Count on two to three months of regular posting. A single video can do very well in the very first week, but steady growth takes time.

### Should I open a business account or a personal one?

For a company, a business account. You get analytics and a link on your profile, with the restriction that you use music cleared for commercial use.

posts.title: AI for social media: what it really does well, and where you're still needed
posts.seoTitle: AI for social media: what works and what doesn't
posts.description: What artificial intelligence does well on social media today, where it gets things wrong, and how to use it without generic text, made-up facts or risk.
posts.excerpt: AI writes fast, adapts a post to each network and suggests topics. It doesn't know your business until you explain it, and it shouldn't answer an angry customer on its own. Here's where the line is.
posts.body:
Artificial intelligence today does a good job of **first drafts, adapting one post for several networks, topic suggestions, hashtags and translation**. It does badly at anything that needs knowledge of your business you haven't given it: prices, opening hours, real photos from your shop, and judging a sensitive situation. The best results come from an AI that knows your brand and a person who approves each post before it goes out.

:::ukratko
- AI saves the most time on first drafts and on adapting posts for each network.
- Without information about your business, **AI writes in generalities and sometimes makes up facts**.
- It can't replace real photos of your own premises.
- Comments and complaints from customers are always answered by a person, or at least a person approves the reply.
- A specialised tool remembers your brand, while a general chatbot starts from zero every time.
:::

## What does AI do well?

AI does some jobs faster than a person, with no drop in quality. These are jobs where the rule is clear and the content already exists.

The first is **adapting**. You have one piece of news, say new opening hours. Instagram needs a shorter text with a call to action and hashtags, Facebook a more conversational one, LinkedIn a more serious one, and Google Business Profile something practical with no hashtags. That takes a person twenty minutes and AI a few seconds, and it sticks to each network's rules as it goes.

The second is first drafts. AI doesn't have to write a perfect text. It's enough that it gives you a good starting point you can polish in two minutes, instead of staring at a blank screen.

The third is ideas and planning. Once it knows what you sell and to whom, AI suggests topics for the whole month, spread across your pillars and days. You throw out the five you don't like and the plan is done. What a good plan looks like is covered in the article on [building a content calendar](@plan-objava-za-drustvene-mreze).

The fourth is the small, repetitive jobs: hashtags, translation into English, a description of a photo for people with visual impairments (alt text), and a summary of the month's results in a few sentences.

!slika:vestacka-inteligencija-za-drustvene-mreze-info

## Where does AI get things wrong?

Its biggest weakness is that it doesn't know what you haven't told it. A general chatbot doesn't know that the bakery opens at 6:30, that a croissant costs 180 dinars (RSD) or that you started delivering last week. When you ask it to write a post, it either writes in generalities (“visit us and see the quality for yourself”) or invents a detail that sounds convincing. **A made-up price or the wrong opening hours** on your profile do more damage than a post that never went out.

The second weakness is voice. Without rules, AI writes the way the average marketing text on the internet is written: plenty of adjectives, exclamation marks and stock phrases. The text is grammatically correct, but it sounds like everyone else's. The fix is a written brand voice with examples, which is covered in the article on [brand voice](@glas-brenda-na-drustvenim-mrezama).

The third weakness is sensitive situations. An angry customer, a complaint about quality, a tragedy in town, a political topic. AI can suggest a calm reply, but a person decides whether to respond and how. An automatic reply to a complaint that gets the tone wrong does damage people remember.

The fourth is real photos. AI can make a picture of bread, but it isn't your bread. Customers can tell, and the networks increasingly label content made with artificial intelligence. **A photo taken in your own premises** still works better than any generated one.

## Table: who does what

| Task | AI | Person |
|---|---|---|
| First draft of a text | writes it in a few seconds | checks the facts and the tone |
| Adapting for several networks | works quickly and to each network's rules | chooses where the post makes sense |
| Monthly topic plan | suggests topics from the brand profile | removes and adds topics |
| Photos | picks stock images or makes a visual from a template | photographs the premises, products and people |
| Comments and messages | suggests a reply | decides and sends |
| Prices, offers, deadlines | copies them from the data it has | confirms them before posting |
| Reviewing results | summarises the numbers | decides what changes |

!slika:vestacka-inteligencija-za-drustvene-mreze-1

## General chatbot or specialised tool?

General AI chatbots are excellent for one-off tasks. The problem starts when you use them to run your social media week after week. Every time, you explain all over again who you are, what you sell and how you sound. Then you copy the text into each network separately, adjust the image format and schedule everything by hand. The time you saved melts away.

A specialised tool remembers. At the start, Sova reads your website and builds a **Brand Brain**, a profile with your services, prices, tone, audience, colours and facts. You can add a PDF about your brand and your own notes. Every post Sova writes relies on that profile and on the brand voice you approved. The text is adapted to each of the seven networks, the visual is made in your brand's style and colours, and the post goes into the calendar for approval. You can see everything that goes into this in the [features section](/#features).

## How do you stop AI making things up?

A few rules apply to any tool:

1. Give it sources: your website, price list, opening hours and a description of your services. The more facts it has, the less it invents.
2. Ask it to write only what the sources say. A good tool does this on its own, but with a general chatbot you have to spell it out.
3. Check numbers, dates, prices and names before every post. It takes thirty seconds.
4. Don't let offers, prices and deadlines go out without a review, even when everything else is automatic.

In Sova, every post waits for your approval by default. When you switch on Autopilot, you choose the level of independence, the token budget and the rules, for example that offers and prices always wait for you, and every post goes through a quality check before it's scheduled. Some networks add their own limits: on TikTok, LinkedIn and Pinterest, Sova doesn't publish entirely on its own but reminds you to confirm.

## Language: Serbian is not English

Many AI tools write Serbian as if it had been translated from English: wrong grammatical cases, word-for-word calques, the formal “Vi” in the wrong places, Latin and Cyrillic script mixed together, and sometimes an English sentence in the middle of the text. Customers notice straight away.

So check how a tool writes in your language before you hand it your profile. Sova writes Serbian in Latin or Cyrillic script, as well as English, and it sticks to one language within a post. Brand details, topics and the call to action are translated, while proper names stay as they are.

## Where should you start?

If you're only just bringing AI in, start with the job that bothers you most. For most small businesses, that's writing posts and adapting them for each network. Let AI write the first drafts for a month while you approve and correct them. After a month you'll see how many corrections it needs and whether you can trust it with more, say weekly drafts based on your strategy.

If you'd like to see how it looks for your brand, enter your website address in Sova and look at the profile and the first suggestions. The trial is [free, with no card](/register). For the bigger picture on running social media, read the [guide for small businesses](@vodjenje-drustvenih-mreza-za-mali-biznis), and for scheduling, the article on [scheduling posts](@zakazivanje-objava-na-instagramu-i-facebooku).

## Frequently asked questions

### Can AI run my social media completely for me?

It can do most of the work: the plan, the text, visuals from templates, scheduling and reviewing results. Decisions about prices, offers, photos from your shop and replies to complaints should stay with you.

### Do the networks penalise posts written by AI?

There's no rule that penalises a text just because AI wrote it. The networks penalise spam and repetitive content, and posts that give people nothing don't perform well. Generated images may be labelled by the networks as content made with artificial intelligence.

### Is it safe to give AI information about my business?

Give it only what's public anyway or needed for posts: services, prices, opening hours, tone. Before choosing a tool, read its privacy policy and check who processes the data. Sova's is on the [Privacy Policy](/privacy) page.

### Which is better, ChatGPT or a specialised tool?

For an occasional text, a general chatbot is enough. For running several networks regularly, a tool that remembers your brand, adapts the format to each network and publishes for you is better, because it saves the time you'd spend copying and explaining everything again.

posts.title: Social media management for small business: a guide from scratch
posts.seoTitle: Social media for small business: a guide from scratch
posts.description: How to run social media for a small business without an agency: which networks to pick, how often to post, what to write, how to measure and the time it takes.
posts.excerpt: What you actually need to do on social media when you run a small business: choosing networks, planning, captions, images, publishing and measuring, with a realistic estimate of the time.
posts.body:
For a small business, managing social media means **two to three posts a week on the two networks where your customers are**, written in your own voice, published when people are watching, with one look at the numbers each month. You don't need all seven networks and you don't need to post every day. You need a rhythm you can keep up for six months.

:::ukratko
- Start with two networks: where your customers are, not where the crowd is biggest.
- Make a **plan for the whole month** in one sitting, in an hour or two, instead of coming up with a post every morning.
- Three types of post cover almost everything: product or service, behind the scenes, useful information.
- Once a month, look at reach, engagement and messages, then change one thing.
- A tool or AI can take over part of the work, but approval stays with you.
:::

## Why does a small business need to be on social media at all?

Customers check you out before they come. They look at Instagram to see what the place looks like, at Google to see your opening hours and ratings, at Facebook to see whether you're still open. A profile whose last post is a year old tells them nobody is minding the details.

The second reason is habit. People buy from the businesses they remember. A bakery that posts every morning at 7:00 to say the croissants are out of the oven doesn't need thousands of followers. It's enough that you think of it when you walk down that street.

## Which networks should you choose?

Start with the customer, not the network. The table below is a rough split that holds for most small businesses in Serbia.

| Type of business | First two networks | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Café, restaurant, bakery | Instagram and Google Business Profile | photos of food, and people looking for somewhere nearby |
| Salon, gym, studio | Instagram and Facebook | bookings by message and local groups |
| Services for companies (accountant, IT, agency) | LinkedIn and Google Business Profile | owners and managers make the decisions |
| Online shop | Instagram and TikTok | short video sells the product |
| Tradespeople and repair services | Google Business Profile and Facebook | people search urgently and locally |

If you're not sure, ask your last ten customers how they heard about you. If three of them say “through Instagram”, you have your answer. How to get found by people searching for a service nearby is covered in the article on [Google Business Profile posts](@google-poslovni-profil-objave).

!slika:vodjenje-drustvenih-mreza-za-mali-biznis-1

## How many posts a week is enough?

For a small business, **two to three posts a week per network** is a good start. That's eight to twelve posts a month, enough for people and the algorithm to see that you're active, but not so many that the business suffers. Regularity matters more than volume: three posts every week work better than ten in one week followed by a month of silence. The numbers for each network are in the article on [how often to post](@koliko-cesto-objavljivati-na-drustvenim-mrezama).

## What should you post?

Most small businesses can work with three types of post that take turns:

1. Product or service: what you sell, what it costs, how to order.
2. Behind the scenes: who works there, how the product is made, what the morning before opening looks like.
3. Useful information: a tip, an answer to a common question, a short lesson from your trade.

These groups are called content pillars, and there is a [separate article on content pillars](@stubovi-sadrzaja). When you run out of ideas, there's a [list of 40 post ideas](@ideje-za-objave-na-drustvenim-mrezama), sorted by type of business.

!slika:vodjenje-drustvenih-mreza-za-mali-biznis-info

## How should you organise the work?

The biggest mistake is coming up with a post on the day. Then every post takes an hour, because first you hunt for an idea, then a photo, then the text. It's better to work in batches:

1. Once a month, in an hour or two, make a **content plan** for the whole month: date, network, topic, type of post.
2. Once a week, film or photograph everything you need for that week.
3. Write all the captions in one go and schedule them.
4. Set aside ten minutes every day for comments and messages.

You'll find what a good monthly plan looks like, with an example, in the article on [building a social media content calendar](@plan-objava-za-drustvene-mreze). Scheduling saves the most time, and the process is described in the article on [scheduling posts on Instagram and Facebook](@zakazivanje-objava-na-instagramu-i-facebooku).

## How do you write so it sounds like you?

Customers recognise template text. “Visit us and see the quality for yourself” says nothing. “The croissants come out of the oven at 7:00, come while they're warm” says everything. Write in specifics: a number, a time, a place, the name of a product.

Set a few rules for your tone, too. Do you address customers formally or casually? Do you use emojis? Which words do you never use? That's your **brand voice**, and it's worth writing down on a single page. The article on [brand voice](@glas-brenda-na-drustvenim-mrezama) has examples and a template.

## How do you know if it's working?

Once a month, look at three numbers: how many people saw your posts (reach), how many reacted to them (engagement) and how many messages or calls came in through social media. Don't check every day, because the numbers jump around from day to day for no reason.

The question at the end of the month is simple: which type of post brought in the most reactions and messages? Do more of that next month. Which metrics make sense and which only look nice is explained in the article on [social media analytics](@analitika-drustvenih-mreza).

## How much time does it take?

A realistic estimate for two networks and three posts a week:

| Task | Time per month |
|---|---|
| Monthly plan | 1 to 2 hours |
| Photos and video | 3 to 4 hours |
| Captions and scheduling | 3 to 4 hours |
| Comments and messages | about 4 hours (10 minutes a day) |
| Reviewing results | 1 hour |

In total, that's **12 to 15 hours a month** when you do it yourself. When someone else does the work, strategy, reporting and back and forth are added, so it comes to 15 to 20 hours. If you don't have that much time, you have three options: pay someone, cut back, or hand part of the work over to a tool. We compare what each option costs in the article on [how much social media management costs](@cena-vodjenja-drustvenih-mreza).

## Where does a tool like Sova help?

Sova takes over the part that eats up the most time: the plan, the text and the visual. You enter your website address, Sova reads your services, tone and colours, makes a plan for the month and writes posts tailored to each network. You review them, correct whatever needs correcting and approve, and Sova publishes them at the scheduled time.

You still take the photos in your shop yourself, because a real picture of your own space works better than any other. You can see how it works step by step on the [home page](/#how), and you can start a trial [for free, with no card](/register).

## Frequently asked questions

### Does a small business have to be on every network?

No. Two networks you run regularly are worth more than five abandoned profiles. Start with the network where your customers are, and add a new one only when the first runs without a struggle.

### Is it better to run social media myself or hire someone?

If you have 12 to 15 hours a month and you enjoy the work, run it yourself. If you don't, hire someone or use a tool that writes and schedules the posts and leaves you only the approval.

### How quickly will I see results?

The first changes in reach show up after a month of regular posting. For messages and customers coming in through social media, count on three to six months, as long as you don't break the rhythm.

### Should I pay for ads?

Not at the start. First build a regular rhythm and see which posts people like. A small ad budget then goes on a post that has already done well, so you take less risk.

posts.title: Managing social media for multiple clients without the chaos
posts.seoTitle: Managing social media for multiple clients
posts.description: How an agency or freelancer runs social media for several clients: account access, a brand voice per client, post approval, deadlines, reports and tools.
posts.excerpt: Five clients, fifteen networks, and each one thinks they're your only client. How to organise access, brand voice, approvals, deadlines and reports so the work doesn't eat your weekends.
posts.body:
To run social media for several clients without chaos, you need **one calendar for all your clients, a written brand voice for each of them, a clear approval flow and fixed deadlines**. You get access to accounts through the networks' official roles, never through passwords. Once that's in place, each new client is a few hours of work a week, and no longer a source of stress.

:::ukratko
- Access to accounts goes through roles on the networks, and the accounts stay the client's.
- **Every client has their own brand voice**, written down on a single page.
- The client approves posts through one link, not through ten messages on Viber.
- Fixed deadlines: the plan by the 25th of the month, approval within 48 hours.
- The monthly report says what worked and what's changing, not just the numbers.
:::

## The biggest problems when you have several clients

The first problem is scatter. One client's posts are in a spreadsheet, another's in Canva, a third's in messages. When a client asks “what's going out next week?”, it takes you ten minutes to answer.

The second is approvals. The client gets a photo on Viber, replies three days later with “fine, just change that word”, and you don't know which word. The post goes out late, and of course it's the person running the social media who gets the blame.

The third is voice. After a month of working for five clients, they all start to sound the same: the way you write. Clients notice.

## Access to accounts: roles, not passwords

**Never ask a client for their password.** The networks have official ways to give access to another person or company: Meta business portfolio (Business Manager) for Facebook and Instagram, admin roles on a LinkedIn page (for example content admin), and users on a Google Business Profile. That way the client can always see who has access and can remove it, and you don't risk being held responsible for their account.

**The accounts always stay the client's.** If the work together ends, they keep the profile, the followers and the history, and you simply lose access. That's fair, and it protects you from misunderstandings too.

## A brand voice for every client

Your first meeting with a new client should end with a one-page document: who the brand speaks to, whether it addresses people formally or casually, three words that describe it, the words it uses and the ones it avoids, and an example of a good post. There's a six-question template in the article on [brand voice](@glas-brenda-na-drustvenim-mrezama).

Alongside the voice, write down the facts: services, prices, opening hours, addresses, and what the client never promises. When you're writing your fifth post of the day, for your third company, you won't have to remember whether the salon opens on Sundays.

!slika:vodjenje-drustvenih-mreza-za-vise-klijenata-info

## How a single post moves through the process

A good flow has five steps, and each one has an owner:

1. Monthly plan: you propose topics by the 25th of the previous month, and the client confirms them.
2. Draft: text and a visual for each network, in the calendar.
3. Approval: the client sees the posts in one place and approves them or leaves a comment.
4. Publishing: scheduled at the right time, in the client's time zone.
5. Report: once a month, with a recommendation for the following month.

The key part is step three. Send the client one link where they can see all the posts for the week or the month, with a preview of how each will look on every network. They leave their comments there, next to the post, rather than in a message with no context. Make the **approval deadline** clear, say 48 hours, and agree on what happens if the client stays silent: the post goes out or it waits.

## Deadlines that save your nerves

**Fixed deadlines** are the simplest tool that agencies neglect. Here's an example that works well:

| What | Deadline |
|---|---|
| Proposed plan for next month | by the 25th of the month |
| Client confirms the plan | by the 28th of the month |
| Drafts for the week | on Friday, for the following week |
| Draft approval | 48 hours |
| Monthly report | by the 5th of the month |

When the client knows the deadlines, they stop sending urgent messages on Sunday evening. When you know them, the work spreads out evenly. What a good monthly plan looks like is covered in the article on [the content calendar](@plan-objava-za-drustvene-mreze).

!slika:vodjenje-drustvenih-mreza-za-vise-klijenata-1

## A report the client actually reads

A client isn't interested in thirty charts. They want to know whether their social media is working and what comes next. A good report fits on one or two pages: reach and engagement compared with last month, the three best posts, the number of messages and enquiries, and one to three recommendations. Which numbers to include and which to skip is covered in the article on [social media analytics](@analitika-drustvenih-mreza).

## How many clients can one person handle?

It depends on the workload, but a rough calculation helps. A client with two networks and three posts a week takes 15 to 20 hours a month when everything is done by hand, as we worked out in the article on [how much social media management costs](@cena-vodjenja-drustvenih-mreza). Once you add meetings, messages and admin, that realistically means six to eight clients for one full-time person.

Tools that write first drafts, adapt posts for each network and schedule them can halve that time. The same person can then run more clients and the quality holds, because their time goes on what a tool can't do: talking to clients, taking photos and making decisions.

## How does Sova work for agencies?

Sova was built for agencies too. You have all your brands in one workspace, and each one has its own Brand Brain (services, prices, tone, audience), its own voice, its own networks and its own calendar. Sova writes each client's posts from that client's profile, so the tones don't get mixed up.

Your team gets roles: owner, editor, client. A client gets an invitation or an approval link, sees the posts exactly as they will look, and approves them or leaves a comment, while you see what's waiting and how much of it there is. Posts go out to seven networks in each brand's time zone, and the monthly PDF report is ready to send. When you turn on Autopilot for a client, weekly drafts arrive on their own, with approval deadlines and the budget you set.

You can see how many brands and networks come with each plan in the [pricing section](/#pricing). If you're curious how AI writes for different brands, read the article on [AI for social media](@vestacka-inteligencija-za-drustvene-mreze).

## Frequently asked questions

### How do I get access to a client's accounts without their password?

Through the official roles: Meta business portfolio for Facebook and Instagram, an admin role on a LinkedIn page, and user on a Google Business Profile. That way the client keeps control and can remove your access.

### How should a client approve posts?

Ideally through one link where they see all the posts for the period and can leave a comment on each one. Agree on an approval deadline, say 48 hours, and on what happens if they don't reply.

### How many clients can one person manage?

When everything is done by hand, six to eight clients with two networks and three posts a week each. With a tool that writes first drafts and schedules posts, more is possible without a drop in quality.

### What should I put in a monthly client report?

Reach and engagement compared with last month, the three best posts, the number of messages and enquiries, and one to three recommendations for the next month. Keep it short, on one or two pages.

posts.title: Scheduling Instagram and Facebook posts: three ways, step by step
posts.seoTitle: How to schedule Instagram and Facebook posts
posts.description: How to schedule posts on Instagram and Facebook: in the app itself, in Meta Business Suite and in a multi-network tool. Steps, limits and common mistakes.
posts.excerpt: Scheduling saves more time than anything else in running social media. Three ways to schedule Instagram and Facebook posts, with the steps, the limits and the common mistakes.
posts.body:
You can schedule Instagram and Facebook posts in three ways: **in the Instagram app itself, in the free Meta Business Suite and in a tool that publishes to several networks**. For one profile and the occasional post, Meta's own tools are enough. When you run several networks or several brands, or a client approves the posts, a multi-network tool saves the most time.

:::ukratko
- Scheduling lets you make a post when you have some peace and quiet, and it goes out when your audience is online.
- **Meta Business Suite is free** and schedules for Facebook and Instagram together.
- For LinkedIn, TikTok, Google Business Profile and the other networks, you need another tool or manual work.
- Check the time zone before you schedule anything for the first time; it's the most common mistake.
- Scheduled posts made through the official tools have no known reach penalty.
:::

## Why schedule posts?

The best time to post is often exactly when you're busiest. A café is full at 8 in the morning, a salon at 6 in the evening, and that's when nobody has time to write a caption. Scheduling splits the work into two jobs: making the post, when you have some peace, and publishing it, when your audience is on their phones. When that is for your profile is covered in the article on [the best time to post](@najbolje-vreme-za-objavu-na-instagramu).

The second reason is **rhythm**. When you schedule the whole week's posts on Monday morning, they go out even if you fall ill, go to a trade fair or simply forget. Regularity is half the battle on social media.

## Method 1: in the Instagram app itself

Professional accounts on Instagram (business and creator) can schedule a post, a carousel or a Reel directly from the app:

1. Create the post as usual, up to the caption screen.
2. Open the extra settings (More options or Advanced settings).
3. Turn on Schedule this post and choose the date and time.
4. Go back and confirm by tapping Schedule.

You'll find your scheduled posts under Scheduled content on your profile, and that's where you edit or delete them. This is the quickest way to handle a single post, but it's awkward for a plan of twenty posts, because everything happens on your phone.

## Method 2: Meta Business Suite

Meta Business Suite is Meta's free tool for Facebook Pages and the Instagram accounts linked to them. It works in a browser and on your phone. Here's how it goes:

!slika:zakazivanje-objava-na-instagramu-i-facebooku-info

1. Open Meta Business Suite and choose Create post.
2. Select where it goes: your Facebook Page, your Instagram account or both.
3. Add photos or a video and write the text. You can tailor the text separately for each network.
4. Instead of Publish, choose Schedule, then pick the date and time.
5. Confirm. The post appears in the Planner, where you can see the whole week and the whole month.

Meta has changed how far ahead you can schedule over the years, and with Meta's paid Meta One subscription the limit is longer than without it. For a monthly plan this isn't a problem. If you schedule a long way ahead, check in the date picker how far it lets you go.

The Planner in Meta Business Suite is good for one business with Facebook and Instagram. **Its limitation is that it only covers Meta's networks.** LinkedIn, TikTok, YouTube, Pinterest and Google Business Profile are left out.

!slika:zakazivanje-objava-na-instagramu-i-facebooku-1

## Method 3: a multi-network tool

When you post on three or more networks, or run social media for clients, a multi-network tool starts to pay for itself. Its advantages over Meta's Planner:

- one calendar for every network,
- text and image format adapted to each network,
- approval: a client or your manager sees the post and approves it before it goes out,
- several brands in one account, with roles for your team,
- statistics for all your networks in one place.

| Method | Networks | Advantage | Limitation |
|---|---|---|---|
| Instagram app | Instagram only | quickest for a single post | everything on your phone, no plan |
| Meta Business Suite | Facebook and Instagram | free, weekly planner | Meta's networks only |
| Multi-network tool | every network the tool supports | one calendar, approval, teams | subscription |

## How does scheduling work in Sova?

Sova schedules and publishes to seven networks through each network's official connection: Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn, TikTok, YouTube Shorts, Pinterest and Google Business Profile. You make a post once, and Sova adapts it to each network. It then goes into the Calendar, where you see it by day and by week.

The time is set in the **brand's time zone**, so a post goes out at 8:00 Belgrade time even when you're working while travelling or your laptop is set to a different zone. If a post doesn't go through the first time, for example because the network isn't responding, Sova tries again and lets you know if it still doesn't work. A client can get an approval link and leave a comment without having an account in the app. How agencies run several clients is covered in the article on [managing social media for multiple clients](@vodjenje-drustvenih-mreza-za-vise-klijenata).

When you switch on Autopilot, Sova prepares weekly drafts from your strategy by itself, within the budget and rules you've set. On TikTok, LinkedIn and Pinterest it doesn't publish entirely on its own but reminds you to confirm. You can see the flow from plan to published post on the [home page](/#how).

## The most common scheduling mistakes

- Wrong time zone. A post scheduled for 8:00 goes out at 2:00 because the account is set to a different zone. Check before you schedule anything for the first time.
- Schedule and forget. If something changes (a price, your opening hours or the situation in town), the scheduled post goes out as if nothing had happened. Look through your scheduled posts once a week.
- The same text on every network. Scheduling doesn't mean copying. Your LinkedIn text shouldn't be the same as your Instagram one.
- Scheduled, but nobody replies. Comments come in during the first hour after a post goes out. **Someone needs to be there to reply.**

## What can't be scheduled?

The networks allow some features only in the app, live. A live stream can't be scheduled like a regular post, and some options for Reels, such as certain music from the library, are sometimes unavailable through scheduling tools. Stories can be scheduled in Meta's tools and in some other tools, but interactive stickers aren't always supported. When a particular feature really matters to you, make that post in the app.

For everything else the rule is simple: the more posts you schedule in advance, the more time you have for the one thing that can't be scheduled, which is talking to your customers. If you're only just putting a schedule together, start with the articles on [the content calendar](@plan-objava-za-drustvene-mreze) and [how often to post](@koliko-cesto-objavljivati-na-drustvenim-mrezama).

## Frequently asked questions

### Do scheduled posts get less reach?

There's no reliable evidence that Instagram or Facebook penalise posts scheduled through the official tools. Reach depends on the post itself and on the reactions it gets in the first few hours.

### Can I schedule Reels?

Yes, from the Instagram app, from Meta Business Suite and from many multi-network tools. Some options, such as certain music from the library, are sometimes unavailable when you schedule.

### How far ahead can I schedule a post?

It depends on the tool. Meta has changed the limit over the years, so check in the date picker. For a one-month plan, the limits are usually not a problem.

### Is scheduling free?

In the Instagram app and in Meta Business Suite, yes. Multi-network tools usually charge a monthly fee, and many of them, Sova included, offer a [free trial](/register).
